intro: SCiPNET SECURE TERMINAL -- SITE-19 / ARCHIVE WING
Read the Level 2 files. Identify the contradictions between them.
Cross-reference your findings. Submit your report.
The work order is open for eleven (11) days from today and closes
automatically at the end of the eleventh. The 'rest' command ends
a day. Days are counted, not granted.
Note: this is a routine assignment. The previous auditor was
reassigned to another division before completing it.

1.title: ACT I — ROUTINE
1.blurb:
Eleven files, one work order, and a supervisor's signature on two incident
reports filed four hundred metres apart. Nothing here is urgent. That is
what makes it work.

2.title: ACT II — ELEVEN SECONDS
2.blurb:
Three incidents in three wings, beginning in the same second and lasting
eleven of them. Five witnesses, counted as six. Something in this building
is keeping time.

3.title: ACT III — UNDEFINED
3.blurb:
An object that can only be described by what it is not, and a division
that writes about it anyway, because writing is the only thing that holds
it.

4.title: ACT IV — SILENT ARCHIVE
4.blurb:
The procedure, seen whole: one institutional name, one credential number,
forty-six closed records, and a replacement posted under the same work
order.

5.title: ACT V — ARCHIVE ZERO
5.blurb:
The archive is not a record of what is contained. Read this far and you
are no longer auditing the documents. You are the thirteenth vote.

days.1:
The corridor lights come up at six. You fetch coffee from the machine on
the second floor, which is the good one. Somebody has taped a note to the
archive door asking people to close it properly. The building is quiet in
the ordinary way.
days.2:
You take the long way round because Corridor B is taped off. Nobody you
ask can tell you what happened there and nobody appears curious. The tape
looks older than any incident it could be marking.
days.3:
A woman in the canteen says good morning and uses your first name. You do
not know her. She does not seem to think this is the first conversation
you have had, and she has finished the sentence and gone before you can
ask.
days.4:
You write the date at the top of a fresh page and then look at it for a
while. It is correct. You check it against the terminal anyway, and then
against your watch. It is the checking that stays with you, not the date.
days.5:
The ventilation runs on a cycle of eleven minutes. You know this because
you counted, twice, without deciding to. On the way back to your desk you
notice how many doors in this wing open only one way.
days.6:
Someone from Medical takes your blood pressure and asks how you are
sleeping. They tick the box before you answer. The form has your
credential number printed at the top and no field for a name.
days.7:
The archive wing has no windows and no clocks, which is standard. What is
not standard is the duty roster, which lists a supervisor for every shift
in the wing and no staff to be supervised. You put it back exactly where
you found it.
days.8:
You find a note in your coat pocket in your own handwriting. It says:
check the number. You check the number. You do not remember writing the
note, and when you look properly, it is not the first one in the pocket.
days.9:
Aksan passes you in the corridor and says, you were right about the second
one. You agree, because it seems unkind not to. You spend the rest of the
day trying to work out which second one, and whether you were.
days.10:
Your signature comes out wrong twice before it comes out right. Not shaky.
Wrong, as though you were copying it from somewhere. The third attempt is
fine. You look at all three side by side for a while, and then you turn
the page face down.
days.11:
There is an appointment in your calendar for this afternoon. Medical, room
4, fifteen minutes. You did not make it. In the notes field somebody has
typed: routine. The rest of the day is clear, and so is tomorrow, and so
is every day after that.

f01_imza.title: FINDING 1 — One signature, two places
f01_imza.text:
Incident reports 173-14 and 096-A carry the same supervisor
signature: V. VURAL. Both are dated 14 March. The two wings are
four hundred metres apart and minimum transit between them is nine
minutes. The incidents were simultaneous.

f02_hayalet.title: FINDING 2 — A signature with no person
f02_hayalet.text:
V. VURAL signed 173-14 as site supervisor. The personnel file
under that name carries 47 signatures and no entry log, no payroll
record, no photograph, no psychological evaluation. The fields are
populated and checksum-valid. They do not read.

f03_numara.title: FINDING 3 — The same number
f03_numara.text:
Your credential number is 19-D-0447-VRL. So is V. VURAL's. Same
number, same division, same work order 4471-B, same date of
assignment: 14 March. A credential number identifies one person.
This one identifies two names.

f04_kilavuz.title: FINDING 4 — Permanent staff
f04_kilavuz.text:
The Archive Handbook states that consistency auditors are
permanent staff with continuous service records, and that no
auditor has ever failed to complete work order 4471-B. V. VURAL
has no service record at all. One of these two documents is wrong,
and it is not the personnel file.

f05_birinci.title: FINDING 5 — First person
f05_birinci.text:
SCP-426 can only be referred to in the first person, and its
archive note records the effect spreading into adjacent documents
during digitisation. The Handbook, digitised in the same batch,
slips into 'I' in its closing paragraph and never corrects itself.
Text is a vector.

f06_hap.title: FINDING 6 — Not an illness
f06_hap.text:
A dose of SCP-500 cures any illness, and one was requisitioned for
an auditor showing cognitive contamination. It had no effect.
SCP-999, which cures nothing, reduces contamination measurably.
What happens to auditors is not an illness.

f07_tarih.title: FINDING 7 — The same day
f07_tarih.text:
Incidents 096-A and 049-C are both dated 14 March and both record
an interruption of exactly eleven (11) seconds. Different wings,
different objects, the same second, the same duration, the same
supervisor.

f08_saniye.title: FINDING 8 — Eleven seconds, three wings
f08_saniye.text:
The camera log shows three cameras in three wings losing eleven
(11) seconds at an identical timestamp. Report 19-Δ logs three
simultaneous incidents in those wings. The seconds are not blank
frames: the frame count is short and the file size is unchanged.
The time was not recorded badly. It was removed.

f09_delta.title: FINDING 9 — The sixth witness
f09_delta.text:
Report 19-Δ lists five witnesses by name and gives the total as
six. It states that the list is complete and the count is correct.
The sixth witness cannot be written down, in the same way the
VURAL file's fields cannot be read.

f10_aksan.title: FINDING 10 — The witness who cannot remember
f10_aksan.text:
Dr. H. Aksan is witness 1 in report 19-Δ. Her own statement says
she remembers the previous auditor's face, voice and how he took
his coffee, and not his name. She noticed the gap months later.
Her memory did not fail. It was edited around a name.

f11_yapayzeka.title: FINDING 11 — What the machine counts
f11_yapayzeka.text:
Asked to list every signatory in the archive, SCP-079 returns 46
names the terminal renders as blank fields, and gives the count as
47 including the credential currently logged in. The VURAL file
reports 47 signatures and zero people. The machine is not counting
signatures. It is counting auditors.

f12_maske.title: FINDING 12 — The role and the person
f12_maske.text:
SCP-035 occupies a host until the original personality is gone.
SCP-963 carries one consciousness into the next body and
overwrites what was there. Both describe a role that outlives
whoever fills it. The archive runs the same arrangement with a
name: V. VURAL.

f13_merdiven.title: FINDING 13 — No floor
f13_merdiven.text:
SCP-087 has no bottom. Every landing is identical and you can
descend forever, believing at each step that you have learned
something. The Handbook describes the audit the same way: read,
cross-reference, escalate, repeat. Neither structure terminates.

f14_kapi.title: FINDING 14 — The same gap, twice
f14_kapi.text:
Eleven (11) seconds are missing from the SCP-1983 breach log, at
the same timestamp as the three dropouts in the archive wing
camera log. The doorway opens onto a place abandoned for a long
time. The same eleven seconds are absent from a spatial record and
a temporal one.

f15_bosluk.title: FINDING 15 — A cause nobody retains
f15_bosluk.text:
Report 19-Δ names SCP-055 as the cause of the incident. The
SCP-055 file can be read and cannot be retained. The archive is
holding the record of an event whose cause nobody who reads it
will still know by the end of the shift.

f16_dokuz14.title: FINDING 16 — The output of nothing
f16_dokuz14.text:
Operation 914-2291 placed nothing in the intake on Very Fine, and
the output compartment was not empty. The output was inventoried
as 'SCP-055 candidate material'. The inventory record exists. The
material does not. The filing officer's name field does not read.

f17_sozcuk.title: FINDING 17 — Written words
f17_sozcuk.text:
SCP-2521 takes anything described in written words, so its file is
kept in pictograms. SCP-055 is held inside what is written about
it, and the writing is the containment. One object is released by
text and the other is held by it. Both make text the operative
substance.

f18_test212.title: FINDING 18 — Two hundred and twelve negatives
f18_test212.text:
Observation Log 055 holds 212 entries recorded over eighteen years
and every one states only what the object is not. The file's own
summary gives the same figure. Two hundred and twelve people
looked directly at it and produced no positive description between
them. The last entries are signed V. VURAL.

f19_wheeler.title: FINDING 19 — The division that writes anyway
f19_wheeler.text:
Marion Wheeler's personnel file has been written and rewritten by
her own department, and carries a standing note in her own hand
telling her to stop if she does not remember requesting it. The
division briefing explains why: you cannot contain what you cannot
remember, so you write, and the writing decays.

f20_ag.title: FINDING 20 — Propagation
f20_ag.text:
SCP-3125 propagates through patterns of thought, and its file
admits sections were rewritten because nobody could remember
reading them. The division briefing prescribes mnestics and
written instruction as the only counter. The containment procedure
and the vector are made of the same material.

f21_site13.title: FINDING 21 — The site that stopped being read
f21_site13.text:
SCP-1730 records Site-13 lost not to a breach but to records that
stopped being read. SCP-079 has read this archive through the same
intranet for thirty-one years and does not forget. It is the only
reader in the building with continuous service, and it has no
clearance to file anything.

f22_sonda.title: FINDING 22 — Who sits with the ending
f22_sonda.text:
SCP-4999 sits with people so that nobody is alone at the end, and
has been observed in the archive wing on forty-six occasions,
always in a small room, always with one person. SCP-093 opens onto
worlds whose records survive and whose people do not. Forty-six
auditors are closed.

f23_magaza.title: FINDING 23 — Structures that rearrange
f23_magaza.text:
SCP-3008 rearranges itself behind the people living inside it, who
build addresses in a store with no exterior. SCP-087 descends past
identical landings forever. Both stay navigable and neither
resolves. The archive index behaves the same way each time your
clearance rises.

f24_protokol.title: FINDING 24 — Silent Archive
f24_protokol.text:
The sealed O5 correspondence says permanent audit staff is
impossible: the text degrades unread and degrades the reader when
read. Protocol SILENT ARCHIVE is that conclusion turned into
articles -- one institutional name, one fixed credential, findings
in, amnestics out, record closed, replacement posted under 4471-B.

f25_sen.title: FINDING 25 — The forty-seventh
f25_sen.text:
Article 5 of Protocol SILENT ARCHIVE states that if the auditor
reads the protocol it has failed, and Article 3 executes at once.
Article 3 closes the auditor's record. Your file gives a date of
termination: 14 March, already filled in. You are auditor 47.

f26_amnezik.title: FINDING 26 — Three doses
f26_amnezik.text:
Your personnel file records no amnestic administration. Your
medical record lists three Class-C doses with dates and a consent
form you signed each time. The handwriting on the third signature
does not match the first. You agreed to this three times and
remember none of them.

f27_son46.title: FINDING 27 — The forty-sixth's argument
f27_son46.text:
Auditor 46 left a note where only the next auditor would look.
They had the whole chain -- rotation, credential, protocol -- and
filed the report anyway. The rotation log gives their finding
count as higher than yours. They knew more than you do, and their
argument for submitting is the best one in the archive.

f28_tamvural.title: FINDING 28 — Forty-seven files, one set of fields
f28_tamvural.text:
With the redactions lifted, the VURAL file is not one personnel
record. It is forty-seven records written into the same fields,
one over another, which is why none of it reads. The rotation log
lists 46 closed and one active. The count matches exactly.

f29_sifirla.title: FINDING 29 — Restore the record, not the person
f29_sifirla.text:
SCP-2000 rebuilds civilisation from stored records and returns the
population without their memories. The 001 proposals are mutually
exclusive files, protected so nobody can know which is true. The
Foundation keeps the record, accepts the loss of the person, and
files its own answer unreadable.

f30_uygulama.title: FINDING 30 — What containment costs
f30_uygulama.text:
SCP-1471 is contained by nothing except being documented and
known. SCP-590 takes other people's injuries into his own body and
then suffers them. One containment costs a file; the other costs a
person. The auditor rotation is the second kind and is written up
as the first.

f31_arsiv.title: FINDING 31 — The archive is the containment
f31_arsiv.text:
Protocol SILENT ARCHIVE escalates clearance without central
approval, because the archive is doing the escalating. ARCHIVE-000
files the archive itself as the contained object: the
documentation practice is the containment, and it holds only while
it is read by someone who does not understand it.

f32_oylama.title: FINDING 32 — Six to six
f32_oylama.text:
The Council has been deadlocked six to six for nine years on
whether to continue the rotation or execute Protocol Zero.
ARCHIVE-000 is the object they cannot agree about. There are
thirteen votes and twelve of them are cast.

f33_terminal.title: FINDING 33 — This session is already logged
f33_terminal.text:
The terminal log holds sessions under credential 19-D-0447-VRL,
timestamps eleven days apart, the same commands in the same order.
Your current session is already in it, and so is a submission
entry timestamped later today. Your file updates while you read
it: fields blank an hour ago are filled in now.

f34_gercek.title: FINDING 34 — The shape of the hole
f34_gercek.text:
SCP-055 can only be described in the negative because there is
nothing in the chamber to describe. ARCHIVE-000 is the shape built
around it. The 212 records are not failed descriptions of an
object. They are the wall, and each one of them is a brick.

f35_vakif.title: FINDING 35 — The writing came first
f35_vakif.text:
The 001 proposal argues that the Foundation exists to keep the
world describable, and that the world was not describable before
it. ARCHIVE-000 states that the archive is the containment. If
both are true, the Foundation did not find the anomaly and write
it down. The writing came first.

f36_gormeyen.title: FINDING 36 — Going in knowing
f36_gormeyen.text:
Task Force Eta-10 enters antimemetic incidents knowing they will
not remember, carrying written instructions from themselves. The
rotation log is the same arrangement run on one person at a time
without telling them. Eta-10 volunteers. Auditors 1 through 46
were posted.

f37_sifir.title: FINDING 37 — The thirteenth vote
f37_sifir.text:
Protocol Zero is a finished operational document with a casualty
estimate, waiting on a vote that has stood at six to six for nine
years. The minutes describe the auditor's report as the thirteenth
vote. What you have been ordered to file is not a report. It is a
ballot.

f38_sonkayit.title: FINDING 38 — It already knows the number
f38_sonkayit.text:
The Last Record was written in advance for whichever auditor
reached it, and it gives a number. The terminal session log gives
the same number for the credential currently logged in. Nobody
entered that number today. It was correct before you arrived.

f39_kurgu.title: FINDING 39 — A history with holes filled in
f39_kurgu.text:
SCP-106's file has holes where three reorganisations destroyed
records no inventory survives. SCP-140 is a book whose surrounding
area quietly reorganises itself to match invented history, and
nobody notices the update because it has always read that way.
One archive loses history. The other adds it, unasked.

f40_1987.title: FINDING 40 — Seven years early
f40_1987.text:
SCP-106 states no record survives of reorganisations 1 and 2. A
recovered fragment of Operation 1's authorisation form, dated 1987,
carries a signature beginning V. V — seven years before the
earliest attested VURAL signature on any complete file. The
pattern is older than the archive admits to knowing.

f41_esik.title: FINDING 41 — A door, not a witness
f41_esik.text:
Three cameras lost eleven seconds on 14 March and recorded nothing
of what filled them. SCP-105's photograph is not a passive record:
a hand reached through one and found eleven seconds of unnamed
texture where a wall should have been. Some recording devices in
this archive may be thresholds rather than witnesses.

f42_hicbirsey.title: FINDING 42 — Every night for eleven years
f42_hicbirsey.text:
Incident 19-Δ places three simultaneous events at 03:14:07 on 14
March. The Wing E guard log shows a printed 03:14 line, filled with
"nothing to report" every night for at least eleven years before
that date. The gap was not new on 14 March. It was routine, and
unnoticed, until it produced something visible.

f43_degil.title: FINDING 43 — Filed by the same hand
f43_degil.text:
SCP-2521 cannot be described in writing and is summoned by written
description. SCP-1425 can be described exhaustively and afterwards
no reader can call its source a book. Antimemetics files them two
shelves apart, opposite mechanisms, the same conclusion: a written
record survives contact with certain things by being renamed, not
by being remembered.

f44_gunluk.title: FINDING 44 — What the doctrine costs its author
f44_gunluk.text:
The Antimemetics briefing states plainly that you cannot contain
what you cannot remember, so you write, and the writing decays. A
recovered notebook shows Marion Wheeler applying this to herself:
eleven years of unremembered requests to leave a division that has
no record of anyone successfully having left it.

f45_trajedi.title: FINDING 45 — Site-19's own hanged king
f45_trajedi.text:
SCP-701's script replaces performers with roles until the company
ledger shows a complete, correctly signed cast that matches no
founding membership list. The unredacted VURAL file shows forty-
seven names occupying one set of fields. Two institutions, one
solution: a role that cannot stay empty consumes whoever is nearest.

f46_devir.title: FINDING 46 — Proof the rule was broken once
f46_devir.text:
The rotation log states no overlap has ever been scheduled between
auditors. A misfiled memo, addressed by an outgoing auditor to an
incoming one under a real first name, proves an overlap happened
at least once, by accident — and something has been erasing the
name from the page, measurably, since it was found.

f47_tahta.title: FINDING 47 — Said without metaphor
f47_tahta.text:
ARCHIVE-000 states that the corpus is a containment procedure held
together by continuous reading. SCP-3999 is the same claim with no
metaphor left in it: a person is overwritten the moment the writing
stops, and the entity's only strategy is patience. Every board in
this archive has been running longer than anyone at it realises.

f48_ondorduncu.title: FINDING 48 — Why the kind option was buried
f48_ondorduncu.text:
A draft fourteenth vote proposed volunteer, informed auditors
instead of unknowing ones, and was withheld before it could be
tabled. ARCHIVE-000's own addendum explains why: comprehension
breaks containment. Informed volunteers would understand what they
hold, and understanding is the one thing this archive cannot file.

f49_esya.title: FINDING 49 — A coat nobody came back for
f49_esya.text:
The lost property log holds a coat, eleven years unclaimed, its
credential field populated and its owner field blank. The credential
matches Archive Consistency Audit's rotation. The unreadable field
isn't only a property of paper — somebody wore this, put it down,
and the paperwork remembers the number and never caught the name.

f50_isik.title: FINDING 50 — Eleven bulbs, every time
f50_isik.text:
The archive wing's lighting fails in clusters of exactly eleven,
on a schedule predating current staff, matching no supplier box
size and no electrical fault. Eleven seconds missing, eleven days
of rotation, eleven bulbs burning out together — the number is a
background condition of this wing, not an event requiring one.

f51_gorusme.title: FINDING 51 — A record that shouldn't exist
f51_gorusme.text:
A researcher reconstructed a conversation about SCP-055 from memory
because no recording device near it survives. Asked whether auditors
undergo the same erosion as the 212 observers, the answer deferred:
'ask it again on a day when I remember today.' The document itself
is proof the deferral is not always total.

f52_anket.title: FINDING 52 — A survey that was right by accident
f52_anket.text:
An anonymous morale question ('I feel my work is understood') has
declined for eleven years in exact lockstep with the shortening
rotation interval in ROTASYON. HR reads it as ordinary turnover.
The department doesn't lose staff to resignation — it loses them to
closure under a name that isn't theirs, measured and ignored.

f53_yedek.title: FINDING 53 — The deadlock was never neutral
f53_yedek.text:
A buried procedural draft shows the Council's six-to-six vote isn't
a fair fight: standing rule keeps whatever was already running in
force by default, so the continuation side needs nothing while the
Zero side needs an outright majority. Nine years of stalemate is
nine years of the same undecided decision, quietly renewed.

f54_saat_yuzuk.title: FINDING 54 — A truth nobody asked for, a lie everyone keeps
f54_saat_yuzuk.text: SCP-4001's timer, wound past sixty minutes, counts down to a stranger's exact remaining lifespan. SCP-4002's ring convinces the wearer of a marriage that never happened. One delivers an unwanted certainty about time; the other manufactures a false one about a person. Neither can be argued with, and removing the ring produces the same grief as the timer running out.

f55_merdiven_sandalye.title: FINDING 55 — Counting changes it, expecting changes it
f55_merdiven_sandalye.text: SCP-4003's stepladder gains or loses rungs only when someone counts aloud, always delivering the climber to the same height regardless. SCP-4004's chair makes a wait feel exactly as long as it was expected to be, without altering the clock. Both objects let perception diverge freely from a fixed physical fact, and the fact never actually moves.

f56_anahtar_pasaport.title: FINDING 56 — Rewriting what already happened
f56_anahtar_pasaport.text: SCP-4005 opens any door once carelessly left unlocked, as if that single lapse were the door's whole history. SCP-4006 causes municipal records to grow a retroactive departure and return to match a crossing that took no time at all. Both objects don't just act in the present; they reach back and edit what "already happened" is agreed to mean.

f57_hediye_album.title: FINDING 57 — Ownership rewritten without a victim noticing
f57_hediye_album.text: SCP-4007's gift retroactively makes a home belong to the giver, and the original owner accepts guest status without distress. SCP-4008's album substitutes a viewer's own relatives into someone else's family photos, and the substituted relatives never notice the gap. Both silently overwrite a belonging record and leave the person who lost something unable to feel the loss.

f58_iade_semsiye.title: FINDING 58 — Two opposite economies of an object
f58_iade_semsiye.text: SCP-4009's return policy erases an object and erases, retroactively, ever having wanted it. SCP-4010's umbrella is never kept, yet always comes back the instant it is needed, its absence elsewhere quietly ceasing to have existed. One guarantees you never miss what's gone; the other guarantees you're never without what you gave away.

f59_sikayet_kartvizit.title: FINDING 59 — Ordinary office items that install control
f59_sikayet_kartvizit.text: SCP-4011's complaint box corrects named staff within 72 hours with no memory of the correction, sometimes making them worse rather than better. SCP-4012's business card makes whoever receives it indispensable to whoever gave it, a dependency the giver never notices. Both are mundane workplace objects that produce obedience disguised as routine kindness or feedback.

f60_gve_yilanbaligi.title: FINDING 60 — Evidence recorded before it could be
f60_gve_yilanbaligi.text: SCP-4013's moths appear in a 1994 photograph decades later, one bearing fingerprints matching a currently active staff member. SCP-4014's final broadcast carries the heartbeat of a diver who went missing nine years before the eel was even captured. Both display information that predates the anomaly's own opportunity to record it.

f61_bahce_fare.title: FINDING 61 — A missing person's trace in an ordinary process
f61_bahce_fare.text: SCP-4015's fruit delivers a missing field researcher's own memory to whoever eats it. SCP-4016's stored nine years of sound conceal a single unidentified voice counting the whole time, underneath the ordinary noise. Both surface a person's trace embedded inside a process that was never meant to record one.

f62_kovan_suru.title: FINDING 62 — Borrowed data replacing your own
f62_kovan_suru.text: SCP-4017's ear-shaped nest answers a question before it's asked, and costs the asker a matching stretch of their own memory. SCP-4018's fused sheep beat with a single heart at a rate matching human rest, not livestock. Both replace something that should be individually the subject's own — a memory, a heartbeat — with something borrowed from elsewhere.

f63_baliketcil_koro.title: FINDING 63 — Two opposite treatments of the dead
f63_baliketcil_koro.text: SCP-4019 holds anything near it in perfect, motionless preservation once acknowledged, having once held six bodies still for fourteen months unattended. SCP-4020 sings with the recorded voices of the drowned, recirculating them as song rather than keeping them still. One freezes death in place; the other keeps setting it back in motion.

f64_egrelti_semender.title: FINDING 64 — Architecture that hides the actual loss
f64_egrelti_semender.text: SCP-4021 erases the reason someone was waiting while leaving the wait itself intact, and the office it happened in often has no record of the reason either. SCP-4022 builds calcified Gothic chambers around trapped prey with narrowing apertures maintained for slow feeding. Both process a victim through an elaborate structure — a waiting room, a cathedral — that conceals rather than performs the actual mechanism of loss.

f65_kopek_termit.title: FINDING 65 — What official records deny and structures confirm
f65_kopek_termit.text: SCP-4023 still greets transferred and deceased staff by scent, unaware time has passed, at a body that has lost 40% of its tissue. SCP-4024's termite galleries mapped a corridor nine years older than a facility's official opening date. Both a dead dog and an insect colony hold an institutional truth more current, or more honest, than the paperwork does.

f66_yedek_akraba.title: FINDING 66 — A vacancy filled the instant it opens
f66_yedek_akraba.text: SCP-4025 adopts a dead staff member's full identity, and was found at a doctor's desk six hours before that doctor's confirmed time of death. SCP-4026 claims the bodies of the friendless dead, always through a differently-named instance, describing itself only as "the one who comes." Both are humanoid vacancies that occupy an institutional role the instant — or before — it opens, one a job, one a family position.

f67_silinen_ilan.title: FINDING 67 — A relationship deleted, a relationship manufactured
f67_silinen_ilan.text: SCP-4027 erases one loved person from a target's memory in the gap of a camera glitch. SCP-4028's death-predicting drafts named an unassigned researcher as his surviving wife five months before she joined his project — and she has since actually married someone else, unremarked. One anomaly deletes a real relationship from memory; the other writes a false one into the record ahead of time and refuses to update it.

f68_kiraci_yara.title: FINDING 68 — Effects that precede their own cause
f68_kiraci_yara.text: SCP-4029's biological age accelerates only when its origin building stands empty, slowing to a near-halt during a squatter's eleven-month occupancy. SCP-4030's camera footage shows an injury hours before it is actually sustained, by a mechanism unconnected to any attempted intervention. Both decouple a visible effect from the moment it should have been caused, letting the outcome run ahead of or independent from its trigger.

f69_yalansiz_kardes.title: FINDING 69 — Forcing reality to admit a truth, rewriting it to make one
f69_yalansiz_kardes.text: SCP-4031 cannot lie and forces a 9-metre radius of honesty around herself. SCP-4032's two dead younger brothers, uncorroborated at intake, have since had a birth record, a school card, and a revised census table quietly appear to support his unchanged account. One anomaly makes reality admit an inconvenient truth; the other appears to be editing records until an account becomes true.

f70_ziyaretci_anlati.title: FINDING 70 — Access to what shouldn't be observable
f70_ziyaretci_anlati.text: SCP-4033 comforts the dying as an exact dead or estranged loved one, and hospital cameras aimed at the visit later show the room empty the whole time. SCP-4034 narrates his own actions 2-5 seconds before performing them, and on three occasions correctly narrated a different researcher's action before it happened. Both demonstrate access to an event before, or despite, any possibility of witnessing it.

f71_tanik_geri.title: FINDING 71 — Effects that don't need the target present
f71_tanik_geri.text: SCP-4035's physically stable body is sincerely recognized by 19 of 22 witnesses as a different specific person from their own past, none of their accounts reconcilable. SCP-4036's compulsive countdown, interrupted with no living target for forty seconds, coincided with three unexplained cardiac incidents 210 kilometres away. Both anomalies' effects reach people with no confirmed direct contact with the source.

f72_kabin_ambar.title: FINDING 72 — A logbook and an ID card older than their building
f72_kabin_ambar.text: SCP-4037's cleaning logbook checks off Stall 4 as cleaned in 1981, six years before the rest stop was built. SCP-4038's grain silo, whose fill sensor has never read positive since acquisition, has yielded the ID card of an employee who vanished from its 1979 payroll with no forwarding address. Both structures produce paperwork contradicting their own official founding date.

f73_kogus_peron.title: FINDING 73 — History that shouldn't have had time to accumulate
f73_kogus_peron.text: SCP-4039's death countdowns follow the patient, not the room, killing them even after discharge to another facility entirely. SCP-4040 is a subway platform showing 40 to 60 years of wear on a line that opened in 2011, with graffiti dated to 1968. Both systems display consequences or history that could not have accumulated inside the timeline everyone agrees actually happened.

f74_asansor_labirent.title: FINDING 74 — What survivors' records never dispute
f74_asansor_labirent.text: SCP-4041's elevator floor runs time at up to 30:1 against the outside, and a phone call placed there arrives hours later in a voice already apologizing for something not yet said. SCP-4042's hedge maze always removes exactly one member from an odd-numbered group, the loss fully remembered and mourned but never once disputed or contested by the survivors. Both structures extract something — time, a person — while leaving behind a record so consistent nobody thinks to question it.

f75_itiraf_fener.title: FINDING 75 — Private truth made public, and made harmful
f75_itiraf_fener.text: SCP-4043 turns a stranger's confessional admission into a line in someone else's obituary, which grieving families accept as accurate. SCP-4044's phantom lighthouse beam leads ships toward hazards that don't appear on any chart, wrecking them on rocks a dive survey can't find. Both convert something meant to warn or console — a confession, a warning light — into public information that ends up harming the very audience it reaches.

f76_kuyu_otopark.title: FINDING 76 — Knowledge of a place never consciously visited
f76_kuyu_otopark.text: SCP-4045's echo answers with information the speaker never said aloud near the well, including a mother's maiden name. SCP-4046 returns vehicles with mileage and debris from conditions the driver has no memory of encountering. Both facilities produce proof of information or travel that happened somewhere the subject cannot recall experiencing.

f77_zil_kopru.title: FINDING 77 — Outcomes fixed before any attempt to change them
f77_zil_kopru.text: SCP-4047 broadcasts a school announcement 40 minutes before it airs, and every attempt to change the wording is erased by unrelated coincidence, restoring the original prediction. SCP-4048 resets odometers mid-crossing and compresses days of driving into minutes, one driver leaving a note about "keeping to the speed limit" she has no memory of writing. Both anomalies enforce a result already decided, making any deviation fail through interference nobody planned.

f78_konuk_kilometre.title: FINDING 78 — Recorded content nobody witnessed arriving
f78_konuk_kilometre.text: SCP-4049 leaves a yearly trail of footprints no camera ever catches forming, and a guest register entry appears even when locked away for the night. SCP-4050's bait vehicle picked up a passenger conversation about a rest stop that exists nowhere on either checkpoint's record. Both are continuously monitored, recurring events that still manage to insert unwitnessed content into their own surveillance.

f79_firtina_merdiven.title: FINDING 79 — Punished for a specific, verifiable error
f79_firtina_merdiven.text: SCP-4051 kills specifically after a verified deliberate lie, striking a fraud suspect and an innocent caddie in the same second regardless of the lie's scale. SCP-4052 claims whoever miscounts landings on both legs of one transit, a missing guard's footsteps continuing past the confirmed top of the stairwell before going to static. Both anomalies trigger on a specific human error — a lie, a miscount — rather than on any physical condition.

f80_tabak_oybirligi.title: FINDING 80 — A shared behaviour nobody had to learn
f80_tabak_oybirligi.text: SCP-4053's entire village independently sets an extra place for an unnamed guest, a custom a newcomer household performs correctly without ever being told it. SCP-4054's zones make every coin and die resolve identically for everyone present, growing to 2.1 kilometres before vanishing outright rather than shrinking. Both are bounded phenomena that install one uniform, unlearned behaviour or outcome across everyone inside them.

f81_gokyazi_monitor.title: FINDING 81 — A record with no source that keeps writing itself
f81_gokyazi_monitor.text: SCP-4055's annual goose formation has spelled out one continuous, unfinished sentence since at least 1954, never repeating a symbol. SCP-4056 logs a fifteenth hospital monitor showing a full, real death on a bed that appears on no floor plan. Both produce a growing, internally consistent record from a source with no physical or biological basis for producing one.

f82_sessiz_kirac.title: FINDING 82 — Interference makes it worse, not better
f82_sessiz_kirac.text: SCP-4057 erases a town's motion for seconds and replaces it with a false shared memory that stabilises faster and triggers a longer second event when the Foundation discloses what happened. SCP-4058's frost pattern predicted a man's death; preventing it for ninety days only delayed it one day, killing him on a stairwell railing the pattern had already shown before anyone noticed the detail. Both anomalies actively punish correction, producing a worse outcome specifically when interfered with.

f83_odunc_sayma.title: FINDING 83 — A population count that never quite lands on zero remainder
f83_odunc_sayma.text: SCP-4059 resurrects a demolished block and its residents for exactly one hour, leaving behind one aged object as the only proof, no occupant ever matching a present-day record. SCP-4060's post-census incident clusters exceed the official population count by one to four every time, without exception. Both suggest that counting or reclaiming a population always leaves a residue that has to go somewhere.

f84_kul_harman.title: FINDING 84 — Something taken silently alongside the main effect
f84_kul_harman.text: SCP-4073 suppresses all sound in its radius, and neighbours confirm nobody heard the fire it came from even before the ash existed as ash. SCP-4074 grants true precognition at the cost of one randomly erased memory per exposure, its urn never losing volume despite 43 withdrawals. Both substances take something — sound, memory — permanently and silently, in an accounting that never quite balances.

f85_buhar_top.title: FINDING 85 — A body unaccounted for by the source facility
f85_buhar_top.text: SCP-4075's facility left behind forty workstations and thirty-nine chairs, and a note calling the gas a treatment rather than a weapon. SCP-4076's fabric holds the exact measurements of one body across four generations of a family's formal wear, and a femur matching that fit turned up packed inside the bolt's own core. Both substances trace back to one specific missing body the source never accounted for.

f86_pas_bal.title: FINDING 86 — A substance that resists its own subject's ending
f86_pas_bal.text: SCP-4077's rust never scaled to anomalous matters until it predicted a named technician's death, then produced a second formation reading only "Not this way" when destruction was proposed. SCP-4078 froze a nine-week terminal prognosis in place for six unnoticed years before an unrelated, mundane death. Both substances behave as though actively resisting the expected endpoint of whoever or whatever they're connected to.

f87_tuz_kum.title: FINDING 87 — Acting before the paperwork catches up
f87_tuz_kum.text: SCP-4079 had already consumed an entire town of 214 people into undifferentiated biomass before the Foundation found it, no evacuation order ever filed. SCP-4080 addresses researchers by name in their own handwriting one to three days before their transfer is finalised in the personnel system. Both substances act on a population or a person before the administrative record has caught up to what's already true.

f88_yag_yabanci.title: FINDING 88 — A consistency the subjects can't compare notes on in time
f88_yag_yabanci.text: SCP-4081 removes every mechanical warning sound before failure, an elevator falling with no acoustic precedent at all. SCP-4082 makes 38 of 41 exposed subjects describe an identical stranger, unaware of each other's accounts, now joined by a second figure only one retired researcher has ever seen. Both produce a silence or an agreement individual subjects have no way to notice or warn each other about before it's too late.

f89_alasim_kefen.title: FINDING 89 — Paperwork that doesn't match the person
f89_alasim_kefen.text: SCP-4083's duplicate count matches the shipyard's storage capacity, not any natural stopping point, and includes 94 copies of an ID tag belonging to an employee absent from every roster. SCP-4084 was recovered from a supplier who filed 23 fraudulent death certificates for bodies never presented for burial. Both substances trace back to a human disappearance hidden behind paperwork that was made to look complete.

f90_ates_cagri.title: FINDING 90 — Separate senses merging into one signal
f90_ates_cagri.text: The volunteer brigade of SCP-4061 reports members dreaming a fire's location before it starts, independently and without comparing notes. The call-center staff of SCP-4062 find their individual voices converging into a single composite voice under sustained stress. Both groups' members' private, separate perceptions merge into one early-warning signal that only exists collectively, never in any one person alone.

f91_orgu_toplanti.title: FINDING 91 — A loss nobody has to name
f91_orgu_toplanti.text: The knitting circle of SCP-4063 transfers members' ailments into the garments they make, worn afterward by someone else entirely. The family of SCP-4064 loses exactly one attendee from its annual reunion every year, replaced without comment. Both groups have found a quiet, ordinary-looking way to redistribute something a member should have kept — health, a place in the family — without anyone naming what happened to it.

f92_dernek_hemsire.title: FINDING 92 — A recurring cost absorbed as routine
f92_dernek_hemsire.text: The civic society of SCP-4065 achieves its public improvements at the cost of one resident going missing per month, a trade its members no longer remark on. The hospice-nurse network of SCP-4066 all hear the identical final sentence from dying patients regardless of the patient's own life or language. Both organisations have learned to treat a recurring, individually significant loss — a person, a dying word — as an unremarkable operating cost of their stated purpose.

f93_inziva_kamyon.title: FINDING 93 — Presence that only appears inside a repeated routine
f93_inziva_kamyon.text: The silent-retreat members of SCP-4067 finish one another's unspoken sentences, a fluency that only manifests during their prescribed silence. The long-haul truckers of SCP-4068 independently report picking up the same phantom hitchhiker, always on the same category of overnight route. Both groups experience a shared phenomenon that only manifests through the specific repeated routine — silence, driving through the night — that their members have in common.

f94_yemekklub_sigorta.title: FINDING 94 — The same transaction in two different registers
f94_yemekklub_sigorta.text: The private dining club of SCP-4069 has formalised a menu that redistributes aging between members and serving staff, priced and scheduled like any other course. The actuarial department of SCP-4070 runs software that predicts individual succession dates with confidence nobody in the office questions aloud. One organisation has written the trade of someone's remaining time into a menu; the other has written the same trade into a spreadsheet.

f95_metro_mezar.title: FINDING 95 — Full attendance as the trigger, not a coincidence
f95_metro_mezar.text: The night subway crew of SCP-4071 only produces its extra, nowhere-bound stop on nights when every rostered member is present, never on a night with a single absence. The gravediggers' guild of SCP-4072, quietly used by the Foundation to detect premature burials, likewise requires its full membership before its detection ability functions at all. Both groups' anomalous or useful effect depends on complete attendance as a triggering condition, not a background fact.

f96_kaset_film.title: FINDING 96 — Overwriting the viewer's relationship to their own past
f96_kaset_film.text: The cassette tape of SCP-4085 dilates the listener's subjective sense of elapsed time around it. The silent film reel of SCP-4086 implants a false memory of having lived through the events it depicts. One medium distorts how long the past felt; the other distorts what the past was. Both leave the viewer's own history less reliable than the recording.

f97_fotograf_radyo.title: FINDING 97 — Content leaking in from outside the frame
f97_fotograf_radyo.text: The photograph of SCP-4087 bleeds architectural detail from a building's true, undocumented layout into whatever image is taken of it. The shortwave broadcast of SCP-4088 predicts a listener's death before any confirmed cause exists. Both media let something from beyond their own frame — a hidden floor, a death not yet occurred — arrive early into the viewer's present.

f98_ekrankoruyucu_kartus.title: FINDING 98 — A harmless loop quietly taking something real
f98_ekrankoruyucu_kartus.text: The screensaver of SCP-4089 compulsively feeds on something from any computer left running it. The game cartridge of SCP-4090 escalates real personal data onto its own death screen with every session played. Both are software media whose apparently idle loop is, over repeated exposure, extracting something genuine from the user rather than merely displaying it.

f99_tablo_kartpostal.title: FINDING 99 — Compulsion the owner can't consciously choose or stop
f99_tablo_kartpostal.text: The oil painting of SCP-4091 replaces the face depicted in it without its owner's input. The postcard of SCP-4092 compels its holder to keep mailing it onward, unable to simply keep or discard it. Both physical media force a repetition or substitution — a new face, a new recipient — that the person holding them never decided to want and cannot decide to refuse.

f100_serit_plak.title: FINDING 100 — An effect indifferent to its original audience
f100_serit_plak.text: The instructional filmstrip of SCP-4093, made for a classroom, produces behavioural compliance in anyone who watches it, student or not. The lullaby record of SCP-4094, made for infants, broadcasts its dream content to any sleeper within range regardless of age. Both media were built for one specific, benign audience, and their anomalous effect has never once respected that original limit.

f101_kitap_telesekreter.title: FINDING 101 — A medium that was never meant to hold this
f101_kitap_telesekreter.text: The children's picture book of SCP-4095 has become permanently haunted by a presence connected to a death nobody intended the book to record. The answering-machine tape of SCP-4096 plays back a griever's own voice to them on command, indefinitely. Neither medium was designed to hold something belonging to death and loss, and in both cases what moved in has stayed for good rather than fading like an ordinary recording.

f102_sunum_bulmaca.title: FINDING 102 — A fabricated history that corroborates itself
f102_sunum_bulmaca.text: The corporate slideshow of SCP-4097 has written a complete, self-consistent false employment history into its subject's own professional record. The crossword puzzle of SCP-4098 substitutes fabricated personal memories for real ones, each clue confirming the last. One medium rewrites a career; the other rewrites a life, but both produce a false history so internally consistent that the subject has no seam left to notice.

f103_reklam_senfoni.title: FINDING 103 — When enough people watch, it stops being private
f103_reklam_senfoni.text: The television commercial of SCP-4099 compels its viewers toward a compulsive preservation of something ordinary, one household at a time. The symphony recording of SCP-4100 produces a mass, identically shared hallucination once enough listeners have heard it together. Below a certain audience size both media behave like ordinary entertainment; past it, they stop being something people privately experience and start being something that happens to everyone at once.

f104_bellek_kayit.title: FINDING 104 — What the body keeps when the mind is edited out
f104_bellek_kayit.text: SCP-4101's operator performs their body's entire task list — calling splits, adjusting lane assignments — while retaining no subjective memory of any of it; the deletion targets interior experience and leaves the physical, externally-verifiable record of the interval untouched. SCP-4102 works in the opposite direction: it rewrites the institutional record and the professional memory of clerks and officials to match a fabricated filing, while leaving the personal, firsthand memory of anyone who actually lived through the period completely intact. Between them the two objects describe a single fault line in what counts as 'real' — one can erase a person's memory of a continuous, verifiable life, the other can erase an institution's memory of an event that was never lived at all, and neither technique touches the half of reality the other one controls.

f105_tarti_yuzuk.title: FINDING 105 — What the body reveals about who you're protecting
f105_tarti_yuzuk.text: SCP-4103 surfaces, on a single unrepeatable use, the name of a specific person from whom the subject is withholding something, encoded as a number that in most cases tracks the days, weeks, or hours since the secret began. SCP-4104 forges an entire shared marital history between two strangers over seven days, while the previous wearer's own memory of that same fabricated marriage quietly fades to background trivia rather than vanishing outright. Both objects treat a person's bond to one specific other person as a quantity that can be externalized and measured — the scale converts a withheld secret into a number, the locket converts an entire relationship into an asymmetric memory load — and neither ever tells the subject what they are being shown.

f106_teyp_ayna.title: FINDING 106 — When the copy stops waiting for the original
f106_teyp_ayna.text: SCP-4105's recordings run ahead of the present, capturing ambient sound from a specific future point that grows more distant with each use at the same site — yet acting on what it records, as in Incident 4105-Kilo, does not prevent the predicted event so much as reroute it into an equally severe substitute. SCP-4106's reflection runs behind the present instead, lagging further the longer its subject stands still, until past seventeen minutes it stops tracking them altogether and begins moving on its own, in three cases leaving a reflected room with no reflection of the subject in it at all. Both objects describe a copy of reality — one temporal, one visual — that is accurate only up to a threshold of delay, beyond which it stops reproducing its source and starts acting as an independent thing with its own trajectory.

f107_en_kisa_yol.title: FINDING 107 — Wishes granted by the shortest path, not the kindest one
f107_en_kisa_yol.text: SCP-4107 routes anyone who walks through its light to whichever surviving lamp of its batch happens to be geodesically nearest and lit at that instant — a purely topological rule that, in Daniel Fitch's case, appears to have routed him not just across distance but across five decades, judging by a postmark the Foundation's own front organization did not yet exist to receive. SCP-4108 grants the literal wording of any typed and removed sentence through whatever sequence of events represents the least overall disruption to reality, a criterion that satisfied ██████'s wish for credit on his novel by way of a plagiarism scandal that ruined his career instead of bringing the acclaim he wanted. Neither object negotiates with the human intention behind the request it fulfills; both optimize for their own impersonal metric — nearest lit node, least disruption — and deliver outcomes that technically satisfy the request while costing the requester everything they meant by it.

f108_dogruluk_araci.title: FINDING 108 — Instruments that read what the subject won't say
f108_dogruluk_araci.text: SCP-4109 requires its White player to remain ignorant of the real-world event their game is nominated to influence, because sessions where the player knew the stakes showed no correlation at all — the object needs a blind, unweighted human input to function as a probability instrument. SCP-4110 needs the opposite: a poured subject who has just truthfully reported their own emotional state, since the locked temperature tracks grief or fear rather than the liquid's actual heat. Together the two objects suggest that reliable anomalous measurement of something intangible — a future outcome, a hidden feeling — depends on the human operator either not knowing or not lying, as though the Foundation's instruments are more sensitive to honesty than to intention.

f109_ekleme_silme.title: FINDING 109 — What gets added and what gets taken away without a record
f109_ekleme_silme.text: SCP-4111 keeps producing new floors above ground level that exist physically — furnished, sometimes recently occupied — but appear on no blueprint, elevator panel, or floor count of the building they're attached to, an addition the architecture never authorizes. SCP-4112 does the reverse: it deletes a specific person from a listener's memory and then, over one to three weeks, edits photographs, records, and even other people's independent memories to match, an erasure the documentary record never authorizes either. Both anomalies run their edits — one additive, one subtractive — entirely outside the institutional or architectural bookkeeping that would normally have to agree to them, and in both cases someone is left aware of the discrepancy: D-11402 finding a ladder already climbed by somebody else, or the forgotten person watching their own erasure happen to them from the inside.

f110_tek_yapi.title: FINDING 110 — Many bodies, one shape underneath
f110_tek_yapi.text: SCP-4114's colony-sites, thousands of kilometers apart, mirror each other's injuries with no propagation delay because the Foundation believes they are not separate worms at all but cross-sections of one organism folded through a non-Euclidean topology. SCP-4113's mats, recovered from unrelated bedrooms with no contact between hosts, independently grow toward the same unfinished floor plan and produce the same shared dream of a house none of the dreamers have visited — one of which has since been matched to an actual, empty residence. Both organisms behave as if multiple, physically separate specimens are local expressions of a single underlying structure that exceeds ordinary three-dimensional space, one stitched together across the seafloor, the other stitched together across sleeping minds.

f111_insan_takvimi.title: FINDING 111 — Animals that keep human time instead of natural time
f111_insan_takvimi.text: SCP-4116's swarm shifts its flight behavior precisely on the hour by civil clock time, adjusting within seconds across timezone boundaries that have no geographic marker, and its floor population rises specifically with leap seconds added to Coordinated Universal Time — a biological population entrained to a bureaucratic calendar patch. SCP-4115's mortality effect runs on a matching 90-day observation window, and regional folklore holds that naming a landing aloud shortens the witness's remaining time, a belief the Foundation's own silence-until-day-90 protocol unknowingly echoes. Neither species responds to a natural cue; both are bound to constructs that exist only because humans agreed to keep time and name events a certain way, as though the anomaly answers to civil convention rather than to the physical world it's embedded in.

f112_kendini_dengeleyen.title: FINDING 112 — Ledgers that balance themselves without being asked
f112_kendini_dengeleyen.text: SCP-4117's remaining bloom count recalculates itself the moment someone updates the deceased's health records in an unconnected database, with no physical or network link between the plant and the archive — the orchid seems to be reading an actuarial ledger rather than a body. SCP-4118's wetland population holds at exactly 340 individuals through 47 years of predation, disease, and deliberate culling, replacing any missing frog within 6 to 19 days regardless of how it was removed, as though the location is keeping a count rather than raising a population. Both objects appear to answer to an abstract number — years owed, individuals owed — rather than to the physical creature or plant in front of the Foundation, correcting themselves against interference at the level of the account rather than the specimen.

f113_ters_isaretler.title: FINDING 113 — Warning signs that point the wrong way
f113_ters_isaretler.text: SCP-4119 makes a fatal wound look and feel healed, generating a false sense of wellbeing that actively discourages hosts from seeking the treatment that would save them, so the reassuring sign is the one that precedes death. SCP-4120's witnesses, by contrast, encounter an unexplained and superficially alarming entity while actually drowning, and their survival rate is nearly triple the baseline for comparable near-drownings — the alarming sign is the one that precedes survival. Read together, the two records suggest the Foundation cannot trust the emotional valence of an anomalous symptom at all: SCP-4119 proves that feeling better can mean dying, and SCP-4120 proves that seeing something frightening can mean living.

f114_sayi_bedeli.title: FINDING 114 — Sentinels that spend lives to keep a count
f114_sayi_bedeli.text: SCP-4121's host mice die on a fixed schedule regardless of whether an anomaly ever triggers the moss's warning response, prompting Dr. Farrow's unanswered question of whether the deaths are incidental to the detection mechanism or part of its cost. SCP-4122's elk are functionally interchangeable with the count itself — necropsies of culled animals find nothing anomalous, and a replacement simply appears within 72 hours to restore the number 217, with the mechanism visibly operating on the herd's total rather than on any one animal's life. Both anomalies treat individual animal deaths as an accepted, almost administrative cost of maintaining a larger function — early warning in one case, territorial population in the other — rather than as an outcome that troubles the system itself.

f115_sessiz_kayit.title: FINDING 115 — Structures that quietly take an impression of what's near them
f115_sessiz_kayit.text: SCP-4123's webs physically encode the ambient sound present during their construction and play it back later, once recovering three fragments of a voice, in a dialect no longer spoken, attributable to no known person present at the scene. SCP-4124's root filaments draw distinguishing biometric and genetic data out of nearby residents over years, producing spore matter that carries degraded but identifiable traces of the very features it is erasing from their bodies. Both organisms function as passive recording media for the humans near them — one for sound, one for identity — and both have, at least once, captured or extracted something that does not trace back to any known, documented source.

f116_bilincalti_tanik.title: FINDING 116 — What the record keeps that the mind doesn't
f116_bilincalti_tanik.text: SCP-4125-1 begins Ms. Sarman's voluntary movements roughly a second before she consciously decides to make them, and on eleven occasions has begun gestures corresponding only to impulses she consciously suppressed — a witness to intention she herself cannot access. SCP-4126's photographs and written logs are the sole continuity of his case, since anyone who looks away for more than three minutes loses all memory of him, the boy himself relying on a personal journal for the same reason. In both cases, an outside record — a reflection, a photograph — retains something about a person's inner life or existence that the person's own consciousness or the minds around them structurally cannot hold onto.

f117_tek_kimlik.title: FINDING 117 — Only one of you gets to have happened
f117_tek_kimlik.text: SCP-4127 forces a documentary and testimonial monopoly on identity: the moment he signs an official document, every record and every memory of the person it names reassigns itself to him, leaving the original person alive but unrecognized by anyone. SCP-4128 shows the same monopoly arising without any external agent — Mehmet and Ali Doğaner share a single set of childhood memories despite having independently lived through it as two bodies, and neither can produce evidence settling which of them the memories actually belong to. Where 4127 externally enforces the rule that a documented identity can only have one occupant, 4128 suggests that shared or duplicated memory naturally collapses toward the same rule on its own, with no institution needed to arbitrate the loser.

f118_bilmeden_yasamak.title: FINDING 118 — Kept from knowing, for the Foundation's convenience
f118_bilmeden_yasamak.text: SCP-4129 is not consistently aware she is a Foundation subject because that fact simply doesn't exist in most of the periods she wakes into, while her body remains fixed at her true chronological age regardless of which decade she believes she's living in. SCP-4130 has never been told that he doesn't age or scar normally, or that he has walked away from six fatal site incidents unharmed, because Directive 4130-Green judges his continued unaware cooperation more valuable than an informed decision he might not make. Both cases pair a documented anomaly of time — a scrambled personal timeline, an arrested biological clock — with a deliberate Foundation choice to withhold that fact from the one person it happened to, for reasons of research or operational convenience rather than the subject's own benefit.

f119_niyet_mi_neden_mi.title: FINDING 119 — Revealing intent or causing it
f119_niyet_mi_neden_mi.text: SCP-4131-1 has, on four occasions, disclosed an action Mr. Keskin had not yet taken but went on to take within 48 hours, and staff have not determined whether it is revealing an intention he holds unknowingly or somehow producing the behavior itself. SCP-4132 produces measurable alterations to physical constants through mathematical notation he invents but does not consciously understand the effects of, reportedly asking why a researcher had "fallen sideways" with no apparent awareness that his own equation caused it. Both records document a Foundation investigation stalled on the identical unresolved question: whether the anomaly is a passive window onto something already true about the subject, or an active mechanism operating through a subject who has no conscious access to what he is doing.

f120_olu_sayilan_canli.title: FINDING 120 — Left dead on paper because it's useful
f120_olu_sayilan_canli.text: SCP-4133-2 asserts herself as Deniz Aksoy, a twin whose civil records confirm died at eleven days old in 1996, yet who recalls a childhood in Rize independently corroborated by surviving relatives. SCP-4134 was legally executed in 2016 according to the facility that recorded his death as successful, and the Foundation has left that status uncorrected because his classification as deceased has been "assessed as operationally convenient" for deploying him on lethal missions. In both cases a legally settled death sits directly alongside an undeniable, staff-acknowledged living presence, and in both the discrepancy stays open not because it can't be resolved but because resolving it would cost the Foundation something it currently gets for free.

f121_tek_agiz_iki_beyin.title: FINDING 121 — Where one mouth ends and another begins
f121_tek_agiz_iki_beyin.text: SCP-4135's spoken translations, when they diverge from the original statement, retroactively overwrite every document, recording, and memory of the event to match her words instead — one mouth rewriting many minds' shared past. SCP-4136 shows the same boundary failing in the opposite direction: Hasan and Nermin Erim produce a single grammatically continuous sentence with individual syllables alternating between two separate nervous systems, their language centers activating 40-80 milliseconds before either one consciously begins speaking their portion. One record is about a single voice overriding a collective memory; the other is about a collective nervous system producing a single voice — together they mark out how thin the wall between an individual's speech and everyone else's shared reality actually is.

f122_gorulmeyen_sure.title: FINDING 122 — Proof only the absent can see
f122_gorulmeyen_sure.text: SCP-4137's extra rooms never appear to the team physically inside the house — they surface only in recorded footage, and only once it's reviewed by someone who wasn't present for the entry. SCP-4138's repeated highway loops likewise vanish from the outside world's clock the instant a driver drops below the threshold speed, yet the vehicle's odometer and fuel gauge keep accumulating the mileage of every loop that officially never happened. Both anomalies produce real duration or extent that is structurally invisible to direct experience and detectable only through a secondary, indirect record — a tape reviewed later, a fuel tank emptied faster than the trip should allow.

f123_sahte_gecmis.title: FINDING 123 — A convincing history that never happened
f123_sahte_gecmis.text: SCP-4139's phantom floors come furnished with cubicles, family photographs, and coffee mugs bearing employee names that match no one in any tenant company's personnel records — an entire fabricated workplace history with no actual workers behind it. SCP-4140 does the same to objects rather than rooms: a wristwatch dropped into the well resurfaces years later worn smooth in a pattern matching exactly the years it was "used," inscribed with the mark of a repair shop that had, per records, already closed. Both anomalies manufacture backstory detailed and internally consistent enough to survive cross-referencing in the overwhelming majority of cases, while leaving a small residue — an unmatched face, an unreconcilable object history — that gives away the fabrication is drawing from a supply of identities and histories belonging to no one.

f124_disardan_kucuk.title: FINDING 124 — More space inside than the walls allow
f124_disardan_kucuk.text: SCP-4141's duplicate parking level B4-A reproduces B4's stall numbering almost exactly, but swaps individual features — a missing fire extinguisher cabinet, a support column with no counterpart anywhere in the real structure — that only someone who already knows true B4 will notice missing. SCP-4142's Recitation Room contains 340 to 400 accumulated manifested objects and structures whose combined described volume substantially exceeds the room's actual 9-by-12-meter footprint, without the excess registering in any exterior measurement Foundation researchers have tried. Neither facility can account for where the extra interior is actually going, and in both cases the discrepancy has already cost the Foundation someone it hasn't gotten back — Agent Halloran on B4-A's ramp system, and, off the books, whatever the Room's non-inert manifestations are now doing on their own.

f125_bosluktaki_fazla.title: FINDING 125 — An extra occupant that fits the gap exactly
f125_bosluktaki_fazla.text: SCP-4144-1 always occupies whichever of Ward 4C's twelve beds sits in the shortest interval of vacancy between one legitimate patient's discharge and the next's admission — an extra thirteenth patient inserted precisely into an administrative seam. SCP-4143's manifestations populate the ghost town with 80 to 110 figures dressed in a style that predates the town's own recorded 1911 founding, an extra population inserted into a gap in the historical record rather than a gap in a hospital schedule. Both anomalies can only be caught by cross-referencing against a system's own paperwork — a headcount against a bed count, a founding date against a costume date — since neither the phantom patient nor the phantom town otherwise behaves as anything other than exactly what it should.

f126_sinir_asilinca.title: FINDING 126 — When the limit breaks, it takes the person too
f126_sinir_asilinca.text: SCP-4145 enforces exactly one crossing per person per day; push past it and the bridge loops you gently back to your starting bank with no memory of the failed attempt — except once, when a resident kept walking anyway and simply was never located again, on the bridge or off it. SCP-4146 excises a confessed transgression cleanly in minor cases, but at severity 8, when Senior Researcher ██████ confessed to excise a mass-casualty incident, the removal didn't stop at the event: eleven years of colleagues now recall no memory of the researcher ever having existed. Both anomalies are quota-based boundaries that work exactly as documented at low intensity, and in their one high-intensity failure each didn't just fail to contain its effect — it consumed the person operating it, with no corroborating trace left behind.

f127_test_edilemeyen_ayin.title: FINDING 127 — A ritual no one dares test to failure
f127_test_edilemeyen_ayin.text: SCP-4147 activates on a fixed count of 137 regardless of who is counting, and the fact that non-counting personnel using the same stairwell see nothing unusual proves the effect is localized entirely to the counting individual's own experience — yet no one has deliberately kept counting to see where the loop actually ends. SCP-4148's Sequence has been performed every six hours without fail since 1994, and the single time it was missed was corrected within 40 minutes, a response too fast to actually confirm what the ritual prevents. Both containment procedures rest on an inferred rather than demonstrated causal link between a repeated human act and an anomalous consequence, and in both cases the Foundation has judged the one test that would settle the question — counting past the loop, or letting the Sequence lapse on purpose — too dangerous to ever run.

f128_esik_sayi.title: FINDING 128 — Exactly three rings, exactly forty-seven people
f128_esik_sayi.text: SCP-4149 activates only when a call is allowed to ring exactly three times and go unanswered, after which a 0.4% probability shift attaches to that line's next call; SCP-4150 activates only in enclosed gatherings of 47 or more, a threshold confirmed as hard rather than statistical when 51 listeners produced onset but 6 did not. Neither trigger correlates with anything the affected humans do consciously — no manual intervention alters SCP-4149's frequency, and SCP-4150's hummers are unaware they are humming until told. Both records treat their numeric gate as arbitrary by any causal account available to the Foundation, yet both mechanisms honor it with total precision, suggesting the count itself is the address, not a side effect, of whatever is listening.

f129_kesilen_hafiza.title: FINDING 129 — A day removed, a sentence interrupted
f129_kesilen_hafiza.text: SCP-4151 removes a single Tuesday cleanly from an entire region's memory, leaving Monday to flow directly into Wednesday with no perceived gap; SCP-4152 does the opposite, delivering a fragment of a dead person's voice that is audible but always terminates mid-clause, 4 to 12 words in, before the thought completes. In neither case is the missing or truncated material itself anomalous — the reconstructed Tuesdays are mundane, and the recovered sentences match nothing the deceased is known to have said — the anomaly is entirely in the act of removal or interruption. Read together, they suggest a shared category of phenomenon whose signature is not what content it withholds but the precision with which it withholds it: a day excised whole, a sentence cut at a word.

f130_izsiz_kaynak.title: FINDING 130 — Ordinary infrastructure, an untraceable sender
f130_izsiz_kaynak.text: SCP-4153 turns municipal streetlight flicker into Morse code predicting emergencies with 82.5% accuracy, and when the Foundation covertly altered a predicted site, the event simply relocated to the nearest matching point in 4 of 6 trials; SCP-4154 turns library catalog searches into phantom entries for books that don't exist, and 34 unconnected patrons have produced mutually consistent false memories of reading the same phantom title despite no contact between them. Both anomalies route information through ordinary civic infrastructure — streetlights, card catalogs — without leaving any trace in the underlying electrical or administrative systems that carry it. The consistency in both cases, a relocated but still-fulfilled prediction, a shared but individually generated false memory, indicates the content is fixed somewhere outside the infrastructure itself, which is merely the channel it happens to use.

f131_yazili_silik.title: FINDING 131 — What is written governs, what is erased still speaks
f131_yazili_silik.text: SCP-4155 shows the Foundation's own paperwork acquiring causal force: a form filed in triplicate, by hand, within one hour, has suppressed reality-altering effects 61 times since 1979, and Dr. Hollis refused to simplify the ritual for fear of what removing its friction would do. SCP-4156 shows the inverse — architectural information that was never filed at all, a mezzanine sealed and struck from the record, a floor removed after a fire, a void marked 'do not disclose', resurfaces anyway, transmitted intact through structurally consistent dreams to residents with no access to the missing blueprints. Between them, they suggest documentation is not a passive record of the Foundation's world but an active variable in it: what gets formally written down can suppress an anomaly, and what gets deliberately left out does not simply disappear, it finds another channel.

f132_dogruluk_bedeli.title: FINDING 132 — Perfect accuracy is never actually on offer
f132_dogruluk_bedeli.text: SCP-4157's emergency broadcasts predict disasters with 97% category, location, and timing accuracy, but every single confirmed instance carries exactly one factual error, which Dr. Voss suspects is the minimum cost the phenomenon must pay to broadcast at all. SCP-4158's thirteenth queue member experiences a completely ordinary transaction that, for every outside observer, consumes 6 to 14 minutes more than it should, with the missing time never recovered by memory or record. Neither phenomenon can apparently deliver a fully accounted result: SCP-4157 trades a fixed amount of truth for the privilege of speaking at all, and SCP-4158 trades a fixed block of time for an interaction that otherwise passes as unremarkable, as though total fidelity is structurally unavailable to either mechanism.

f133_bilinmeyen_esik.title: FINDING 133 — Nobody notices the number they're obeying
f133_bilinmeyen_esik.text: SCP-4159's audiences applaud for exactly 17 seconds beyond the natural decay of clapping, in perfect unison, then stop simultaneously with no member aware of having done anything unusual — control audiences shown fabricated footage of the same length do not even develop false confidence about it. SCP-4160's municipalities keep their population counts from ever reaching a specific excluded integer, through growth that flattens or single-cycle drops with no corroborating record of the deaths or departures cited, while local officials and residents show no awareness of participating in the correction. Both records describe a precise number governing collective behavior — a duration, a population ceiling — that is honored exactly by everyone involved and understood by no one involved, its significance legible, if at all, only to whatever is on the other side of the threshold.

f134_gizli_borc.title: FINDING 134 — Every granted wish has an uncredited debtor
f134_gizli_borc.text: SCP-4161's knitting circle turns a spoken wish and hand-spun hair into a granted outcome, but drains the hair donor's autobiographical memory at roughly forty minutes per hour of knitting, a cost the donor never learns of. SCP-4162's arbitration board turns a signed ruling into rewritten physical and documentary reality, but extracts a proportionate, undisclosed cost from the panelists who signed it — a divorce, a lost pregnancy, an unexplained estrangement — within the following year, none of it recognized by the panelist as connected to the vote. Both records describe reality-bending outcomes delivered through completely mundane civic or social ritual, a hobby circle, a jury duty rotation, that quietly bills someone who never agreed to pay and never learns they did.

f135_kendi_tasiyicisi.title: FINDING 135 — The pattern finds its next carrier on its own
f135_kendi_tasiyicisi.text: SCP-4163's forum somehow finds each new symptomatic dreamer through search terms despite being absent from all indexed results, and its 'In Memory' thread updates with a departed member's name within hours of their final post, before any living member notices the absence. SCP-4164's inheritance skips any firstborn who dies before onset and passes instead to the next living firstborn in eligible descent, indicating a single continuous process seeking a body rather than independent triggers in each individual. Neither phenomenon depends on deliberate transmission between hosts — both appear to actively locate, track, and reassign their next carrier on their own, with a bookkeeping precision, an unindexed forum found anyway, a bloodline followed past a death, that none of the affected individuals, or the Foundation, can account for.

f136_uyelik_korlugu.title: FINDING 136 — Membership comes with a blind spot built in
f136_uyelik_korlugu.text: SCP-4165's newly confirmed partners permanently lose the ability to perceive arithmetic discrepancies that are multiples of $47,000, a blindness that persists even after they retire and does not lift retroactively. SCP-4166's Congregation members are never told the restricted name at all during their active membership, and only receive it, in exchange for a proportionate loss of their own memory, at the moment they formally leave. Both anomalies gate a specific piece of knowledge to a specific point in a person's relationship with the group: SCP-4165 seals it permanently at the moment of joining, while SCP-4166 releases it, at a cost, only at the moment of leaving, suggesting institutional membership itself is what the anomaly is tracking, not any individual's choices within it.

f137_mudahale_etmeme.title: FINDING 137 — Everyone involved knows, and no one stops it
f137_mudahale_etmeme.text: SCP-4167's thirteen bus-accident survivors could, per Foundation offer, seek medical investigation into the mechanism forcing their twenty-one-day meetings, but decline every time, citing an unexplained shared certainty that stopping would be 'worse.' SCP-4168's law society initiates could, in principle, warn a nominee, refuse a naming, or intervene for a person they have already erased, but no member has ever been observed attempting any of it across the Society's recorded history. Neither anomaly is sustained by ignorance — both sets of participants understand, at least partially, what is happening to them or because of them — but by a consistent, voluntary choice not to interfere, as though every person involved has independently concluded that resistance carries a worse cost than compliance.

f138_biriktirilemez_koruma.title: FINDING 138 — Safety here is spent, never saved
