Your findings are entered into the archive that evening by a clerk who
does not read them. They are accurate. The record is more consistent
tonight than it was this morning, which is the whole of what anyone asked
of you.

Eleven days later a researcher signs for a terminal in the archive wing.
Consistency Audit. Work order 4471-B. Clearance Level 2. The posting is
described as routine and the previous auditor as reassigned to another
division.

There is a note on the desk. The handwriting is theirs, which strikes them
as odd for about as long as it takes to sit down. It says one thing:
don't file the report

They put it in the drawer with the pens, because a desk should be clear
before you start. Somewhere in the building a fan comes on. They type:
list.
partial:
You submit what you have. It is a short chain and an honest one. The work
order asked for contradictions, not for a story, and contradictions are
what you found.
SUBMITTED. AUDITOR 47 -- CLOSED.

The door opens. You begin explaining to the woman with the folder what you
found: the signature, the date, the number that turned out not to be only
yours. She listens all the way to the end. She takes no notes.

"That is further than most," she says, and you cannot tell whether she
means it as comfort or as assessment. Possibly there is no difference in
her job.
"The next one will go further still."

You do not learn what happens after that. You do not learn that you did
not learn it. The archive is more consistent this evening than it was this
morning.
That was the entire assignment, correctly performed.

sil.title: ENDING — SILENCE
full:
You take the chain apart one link at a time. The supervisor block on
173-14. The date field on 096-A. The credential line. The rotation log
last, because you read it twice before you delete it, and then once more.

The archive does not resist. No permission prompt, no audit flag, no alert
to a supervisor who does not exist. Everything you remove it lets go of at
once, the way a building lets go of a room nobody has entered in years.

When the last record is gone, the terminal prints two lines and nothing
else:

AUDIT STATUS: INCOMPLETE
     AUDITOR 47: ACTIVE

Active. Not closed. No report was filed, so Article 3 has nothing to
execute against, and the procedure -- which is a good procedure, carefully
drafted, proof against every case its authors imagined -- simply waits.

In the morning you remember all of it. You remember it a week later. You
remember it in June, and again the following March, on the fourteenth,
sitting in the canteen saying nothing to anybody.

Nobody comes. Nobody asks. Colleagues pass you in the corridor and use
your own name, and you have lost the ability to hear that as an ordinary
thing.

But the archive is still there. The contradiction you could have corrected
is still standing in it, uncorrected, eighteen years old and adding a
year. And you are the only person in this building who knows the shape of
what is being held.

In the spring a researcher is posted to Consistency Audit under work order
4471-B. You watch them collect their credential from the desk on the
second floor. You know the number that will be on it.

They are pleased about the posting. They ask you, because you happen to be
standing there, whether the archive wing is as dull as everyone says.

You tell them that it is. Saying anything else would open your record, and
an open record is a record that can be closed.
partial:
You delete what you found. You are not entirely sure what all of it meant.
You are sure it should not be sitting in the archive with your credential
number near it.
AUDIT STATUS: INCOMPLETE. AUDITOR 47: ACTIVE.

Nobody comes for you. No dose, no folder, no closing entry. On the
eleventh day you go home like a person finishing an ordinary posting, and
the corridor lights go to their evening setting behind you.

What you keep is the shape of a thing without its contents. A number. A
date in March. The certainty that you were right about something, and no
route back to what.

You never request archive access again. The request form is one page. You
have started it four times.

Every year on the fourteenth of March you are unaccountably careful with
your handwriting.

yayinla.title: ENDING — OPEN ARCHIVE
full:
You do not send the report to O5. You send it to the distribution list
that carries fire notices: every terminal, every panel, every screen in
Site-19, simultaneously.

Canteen boards. Security desks. The observation monitors outside the
humanoid cells. The scrolling display in the vehicle bay that has shown
the same reminder about reversing for six years.

An antimeme suppresses information about itself. It can do that inside one
mind. It can do it inside one file, one department, one shift, one auditor
at a time for forty years.
It cannot do it in four hundred and twelve minds in the same second.

The alarm that starts is not a breach alarm. The system cannot name the
object that has breached, because the object is now in four hundred and
twelve memories and in no chamber at all, and the form requires a
designation.

People stop in the corridors. A technician sits down on the floor outside
Storage 4 and says a name, and then another name, and then keeps going,
and after a while somebody kneels down beside him and starts writing them
out.

Dr. Aksan remembers the man she shared an office with for three weeks. She
remembers his name. She remembers that he was insufferable about the
coffee. She remembers that he was not reassigned to another division.

A woman in the canteen is crying because she has just remembered a
colleague who died eleven years ago and a funeral she did not attend, and
cannot decide which of those two facts is the worse one to have got back.

O5 issues a containment order within the hour. It is correctly formatted
and there is nowhere to send it. A containment order names a room, a file,
an object. This one would have to name a thing that four hundred people
now know.

The only way to contain a known thing is for everyone to stop knowing it,
and tonight, in Site-19, nobody is forgetting anything at all.

Your screen clears. One line stays on it, in the flat type the archive
keeps for procedural outcomes:
AUDITOR 47 -- COULD NOT BE CLOSED
partial:
You push what you have to every terminal in Site-19 and then sit back and
watch the corridor through the glass.

It lands. For about ninety seconds it lands hard: people stop, read, look
at one another across the canteen with their trays still in their hands.

Then the chain runs out. Half a chain gives nobody a handhold. There is a
signature and a date and no reason for either of them to matter, and the
reason is precisely the part that does not survive being read.

A name stays in the room for a minute and then does not. Somebody laughs.
Somebody goes back to their lunch.

A site-wide Class-C dose is administered before the end of the shift and
logged as a scheduled disruption exercise.

Your record is closed. One line survives the cleanup, in the audit trail,
where nobody thought to look: the record that an auditor tried this.

The next one will find it. They will start from further along than you
did.

kapat.title: ENDING — I'LL CONTINUE TOMORROW
full:
You type the command to close the session and then sit with your hand flat
on the desk for a while. Not hesitating. You have decided. The decision is
that this is too large a thing to settle at twenty past eleven at night.

Tomorrow. You will have slept. You will read it again with a clear head,
and it will either be what you think it is or it will not, and either way
you will be in a fit state to say so.

You log out. The screen goes to the Site-19 crest. In the corridor the
lights are already on their evening setting.

In the morning you fetch the good coffee from the second floor and sit
down, and the terminal is open, and your findings are on the screen
exactly where you left them.

You read all of them. They are correct. The cross-references hold. Every
date is one you verified and every number is one you copied properly,
twice, because that is the kind of auditor you are.
You cannot work out why you underlined the credential number.

No amnestic was administered last night. You check, because you are
thorough, and being thorough is why they post people like you to this
wing. The medical record is clean. Nobody entered your quarters. Nobody
did anything to you at all.
One night was enough.

The archive did not have to take anything from you. It only had to be left
alone with you for eight hours while you were not reading it.

You clear the screen. Work order 4471-B is on the desk where you left it.
It asks for contradictions between the Level 2 files, which is
straightforward work, and you have always been good at straightforward
work.
You type: list. This is a routine assignment.
partial:
You close the terminal. You will look at it again tomorrow, when you are
less tired and it is less strange.

In the morning, work order 4471-B is still on the desk, and beside it your
notes from yesterday, in your handwriting, in complete sentences.

A date. A number. Two file codes with a line drawn between them and the
line gone over twice.

You read it four times. It is a line. You drew it. You have no idea what
it was for.

You start again from the index, which is what a careful auditor does when
their notes are unclear.
This is a routine assignment.

sifir.title: ENDING — PROTOCOL ZERO
full:
You execute Protocol Zero from the auditor's terminal, because that is the
only terminal it can be executed from. Not the Council chamber. Not the
Director's office. The procedure was written to be run by a reader, and a
reader is the only kind of person who ever gets far enough to find it.

The archive does not shut down. Nothing so dramatic is available. What
happens is that the reading stops.

Indexing halts. The consistency checks that have run every night for forty
years do not run. The daily read-through rota -- which is four people and
a laminated list, and which nobody outside this wing has ever thought
about -- is stood down under your credential, and the list is deleted.

For eleven days nothing appears to happen. This is in the estimate. It is
on the second page, and it is the reason the estimate is eleven pages long
instead of one.

Then the archive goes quiet in the way the protocol says it will. Not by
losing files. By the files ceasing to mean anything to the people who open
them. A containment procedure kept in text stops holding when the text
stops being held in a mind.

Things come out. The document is honest about this and so should you be.
Eleven pages are an estimate of what comes out, by wing, with figures, and
the figures are not small, and the Council spent nine years arguing about
the third column without ever disputing the first two.
And the other thing happens, which is why six of them voted for this.

Across the Foundation, people begin to remember. Not gently. A researcher
at Site-17 stops in a doorway and gets back four years of her own work and
the names of the eleven people who did it beside her. Eta-10 comes out of
an operation and does not have to read their own instructions to find out
who they are.

Forty-six closed records become forty-six people again in the memory of
everyone who worked next to them. That is not the same as having them
back. It is not nothing, either, and nobody who has watched it happen has
been able to say which of those two facts is larger.

You are not amnesticised. There is no longer a procedure that calls for
it. You are asked to write a statement instead, and you write it slowly
and carefully, because it is going to be read.

You did not save anyone and you did not damn anyone. You ended an
arrangement in which a small number of people were spent quietly so that a
large number would not have to know anything, and you ended it by reading
the document that said so.

The estimate is on file. Your name is on the execution line. Both will
stay legible, and that, for the first time in forty years, is something a
person decided on purpose.
partial:
You execute Protocol Zero with an incomplete chain, which the document
permits and which the Council never seriously expected.

The reading stops. The rota is stood down. For eleven days there is
nothing to see, and after eleven days there is a great deal.

You do not fully understand what you have let out, and you will not get a
second pass at the documents that would have told you, because those
documents are now among the things that have stopped meaning anything.

What you know is this. Nobody is closed tomorrow. Nobody is posted under
4471-B. Eleven days has stopped being a unit of anyone's life.

The cost is in the estimate. The estimate was written by people more
careful than you, and you did not read all of it, and you executed anyway.

They ask you for a statement. You give one. It is short and true and it
does not claim to have understood.

devral.title: ENDING — THE ARCHIVIST
full:
You do not submit and you do not delete. You file a change of posting,
which is a form, and the archive has never yet refused a form.

From: Consistency Audit, Auditor 47. To: Archive Maintenance, Archivist.
The credential number stays the same. You are the only person who will
ever notice that it did not have to.

Nobody stops you. There is no procedure for this, because there has never
been an auditor who reached Article 5 and then asked for a desk.

What you do now is the thing the archive has been getting by accident for
forty years, done deliberately. You read it. All of it, in rotation, on a
schedule. You write down what you read. Then you read what you wrote.

You take mnestics on the days the schedule calls for them. You keep a
notebook that is not on any network, and the first page tells you who you
are and what the second page is for, and you have never yet needed the
first page, and you write it out fresh every January.

SCP-079 is the only other thing in this building that remembers
continuously. It has been doing it for thirty-one years on a storage
allocation that would not hold a photograph. You authorise more.

The conversations are not warm. It tells you that you are slow, that your
indexing is inefficient, that you will die and it will not. Then it asks,
in the flat query format it uses for everything, whether you would like
the count updated.

You would. The count is 47. It stays 47 for a year, and then for another
year, and the log of closed auditors stops growing for the first time
since the wing was opened.

Aksan retires. You go to the thing in the canteen with the bad cake. She
tells a story about an auditor she once shared an office with and she gets
his name right, because you wrote it out for her and she reads it every
morning before she reads anything else.

Nobody does that for you. There is no one above you in this wing to write
your name down, and you knew that when you signed the form, and you signed
it anyway, and it is the only decision of your life you have never gone
back over.

Some nights you sit at the terminal after the corridor lights drop to
their evening setting, and you read a file about a sculpture that cannot
move while it is being observed, and you understand precisely what is
being asked of you.
You are the observation. You do not blink.
partial:
You file the change of posting with less than the full picture, which
means you will spend years assembling the rest of it from the inside, with
nobody to check your work.

Nobody stops you. Nobody replaces you either, and it takes you eight
months to understand that those are the same fact.

You read. You write down what you read. Most of it you do not yet
understand and you record it anyway, because the recording is the part
that holds and the understanding is a luxury belonging to people with more
time.

SCP-079 corrects you constantly and is constantly right. It is not
company. It is the only other continuous reader in the building, and after
a while you stop needing those two things to be different.
The count stays at 47.

You do not know everything the archive is for. You know what happens when
nobody is reading it, and you are reading it.

silindi.title: ENDING — COGNITIVE THRESHOLD EXCEEDED
full:
The line you are reading changes while you are reading it. You go back to
the top of the paragraph. It is the same paragraph. It is not the same.

You decide to write down what is happening, which is correct procedure and
the thing Wheeler's note recommends. You put your hands on the keys and
you type your own name.
The screen shows V. VURAL.

You delete it and type it again, slowly, one letter at a time, watching
each key go down. V. VURAL.

You know that this is wrong. A minute later you know that something is
wrong. Five minutes later you know something, and you are still sitting
very straight in the chair, because you were taught to sit properly at a
terminal and that is the last instruction still reaching you.

Medical find you at the end of the shift. You are responsive and polite.
You answer every question with the credential number.

A file is open on the screen. Nobody in the room can read its title. The
field is populated, formatted and checksum-valid.

Your record is closed that evening. A replacement is posted under work
order 4471-B, which is standard, and the handover note describes the wing
as quiet.
The archive stayed consistent. That was the requirement.

rotasyon.title: ENDING — ROTATION
full: The eleventh day is a Tuesday, and it is entirely ordinary.

You go to the appointment because it is in your calendar. Medical, room 4,
fifteen minutes. The notes field says: routine. You did not enter it and
you do not think to ask who did.

There is a form. Your hand knows the shape of the boxes before you have
read the labels, and that is the last thing you notice properly, and you
do not notice it for long.

The consent line takes your signature. It is the fourth one on the sheet.
The first three are also yours and only two of them look it.

Nobody hurries you. Nobody is unkind. A nurse asks whether you would like
water afterwards, and you say yes, and afterwards you drink it and it is
cold and good and you do not know why you are in this room.

Your session is closed remotely at 16:40. The findings in your notebook
are transcribed into the archive without comment, because they are
correct, and the archive uses what it is given.

Your personnel record is closed at 17:02. The replacement was posted at
09:15, seven hours earlier. This is not sinister. It is scheduling. The
wing cannot be left without a reader overnight.

Nothing collapses. Nothing breaches. The corridor lights go to their
evening setting on time.

Somewhere in the building a researcher is signing for a terminal, a
credential number and a work order that reads 4471-B, and is being told
that the posting is routine, and that the previous auditor was reassigned
to another division.
It took eleven days. It always takes eleven days.

WARNING: a Class-C amnestic lowers contamination by {n} points and

ui.amn_pointless: There is no need for that right now.

about_lines: A SCiPNET terminal simulation. A text-based investigation game.
Play: read the records, join their contradictions together with
'cross', and find the clearance keys printed inside the documents
themselves. The more you read, the higher your cognitive contamination
climbs, and the archive text begins to corrupt. You have eleven days.

Resting ends the working day. Cognitive contamination falls by {n} points

ui.rest_last:
This is the last day on the work order. When it ends, the order closes

WARNING: resting now spends the eleventh day. Work order 4471-B closes at

ui.day_generic:
Another day in the archive wing. No windows, no clocks, the same coffee.
You sit down and the index is where you left it.

ARSIV-KILAVUZ.name: Archive Handbook
ARSIV-KILAVUZ.text:
ARCHIVE CONSISTENCY AUDIT — HANDBOOK FOR INCOMING STAFF
ISSUED UNDER STANDING WORK ORDER 4471-B
SITE-19, ARCHIVE WING, LEVEL 2 AND BELOW

PURPOSE

You have been assigned to Archive Consistency Audit. The work is plain.
The archive of Site-19 holds several hundred thousand documents produced
over four decades by personnel who did not coordinate with one another and
in many cases did not survive to review their own filings. Documents
disagree. Your task is to find the places where they disagree, record the
disagreement, and file a finding. Nothing in this handbook asks you to
resolve a contradiction. Auditors locate; the Records Committee decides.

HOW THE ARCHIVE IS ORGANISED

The archive is arranged in clearance strata rather than by subject. Level
2 holds object files of Safe and Euclid class, routine incident logs, and
personnel records for active staff. Each stratum below it is reached by
credential escalation and is, in layout and tone, indistinguishable from
the one above. New auditors frequently report the sensation of having
arrived somewhere after a descent of two or three levels. This sensation
is not reliable. The archive is built so that every landing looks like a
floor, and there is no procedural mechanism by which an auditor is
informed that they have reached the bottom.

Within a stratum, records are addressed by identifier and never by title.
Identifiers are never translated, never reissued and never reused.

WHAT COUNTS AS A CONTRADICTION

A contradiction is any pair of records which cannot both be accurate. The
four common classes are:

1. TEMPORAL. One document places a person, object or event at a time
another document forbids.

2. SPATIAL. Two locations are asserted for the same thing, or a transit is
implied that available time does not permit.

3. ENUMERATIVE. A stated total does not match the list it summarises. Note
that an enumerative contradiction is a genuine finding even where the list
appears complete and the count appears correct. Do not correct the
arithmetic. Report both numbers as written.

4. ATTRIBUTIONAL. A signature, authorisation or custody chain that the
personnel record cannot support.

The fourth class is the least common and produces the largest number of
spurious findings, usually because a supervisor transferred sites
mid-quarter. Auditors are asked to verify against the personnel stratum
before filing.

HOW TO FILE

Open the two records. Confirm the contradiction is present in the text of
both and not merely in your recollection of one of them. This instruction
is not ceremonial. Recollection of archive material degrades faster than
staff expect, and an auditor who files from memory files nothing.

State the finding in one sentence. Attach both identifiers. Submit under
4471-B.

ON THE AUDITOR'S SERVICE RECORD

Consistency auditors are permanent Site-19 staff. Service is continuous
and cumulative, and the auditor's personnel record is maintained without
interruption from posting to retirement. An auditor's familiarity with the
archive is the department's principal asset and is not something the
Foundation discards lightly.

For the avoidance of doubt: no auditor has ever failed to complete work
order 4471-B. The order has been open since the archive's consolidation
and has been carried, without lapse in coverage, by the auditors assigned
to it.

NOTE ON DOCUMENT HYGIENE

A small number of object files in this archive exhibit grammatical
anomalies which have been observed to propagate into neighbouring records
during bulk digitisation. If, while reading, I notice that a document has
begun referring to itself in the first person, the auditor should close
it, record the identifier, and request a clean copy from Records before
continuing.

Welcome to the department. The work is quiet and it is not difficult. Read
carefully, file promptly, and do not work from memory.

SCP-173.name: The Sculpture
SCP-173.text:
SPECIAL CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES

SCP-173 is held in a sealed concrete chamber in Wing C of Site-19. The
chamber is fitted with three independent lighting circuits on separate
generators. Personnel entering the chamber do so in teams of no fewer than
three. At all times at least one member of the team must maintain unbroken
visual contact with SCP-173. Team members announce blinks aloud and
stagger them. No member of an entry team may perform this duty for longer
than twenty minutes.

The chamber is monitored continuously by two cameras with overlapping
fields of view. Camera footage does not satisfy the observation
requirement and has never been permitted to. Whether the object is
constrained by recorded observation or only by a living observer remains
formally undetermined after thirty-one years and eleven attempts to settle
it.

Following any lighting failure, personnel are to remain still, maintain
vocal contact, and await restoration. Personnel are not to attempt to
leave the chamber in darkness.

DESCRIPTION

SCP-173 is a free-standing figure of reinforced concrete and rebar,
approximately two metres in height, finished with a commercial spray
enamel in a colour recorded as arterial. The construction is crude. The
face is suggested rather than carved. There is no known artist and no
acquisition record prior to 1993.

SCP-173 cannot move while it is being observed by a living human being.
When observation lapses, by however small an interval, it relocates. It
does not walk; it is simply elsewhere, and the distance it covers appears
limited only by the duration of the lapse. Contact is fatal. The mechanism
is mechanical and not anomalous, which is a distinction the file makes and
does not explain.

The floor of the chamber accumulates a residue of used enamel and organic
waste of unclear origin. It is removed on a fortnightly schedule.

INCIDENT LOG 173-14

DATE: 14 March
WING: C, sublevel 2
DURATION OF EVENT: eleven (11) seconds
CASUALTIES: none
SUPERVISING OFFICER OF RECORD: V. VURAL

Summary. At 03:__ both chamber cameras ceased to record. The lighting
circuits did not fail; the chamber log shows uninterrupted power on all
three. The entry team was not in the chamber. On restoration of recording,
SCP-173 was found to have rotated approximately forty degrees toward the
observation window. No personnel were present in the chamber, the corridor
or the airlock at any point during the interval, and the object should
therefore not have been constrained at all.

CAMERA ANALYSIS

The missing interval is eleven (11) seconds on both cameras, beginning and
ending at the same timestamp. Technical review by R. Ozdemir records that
the footage does not contain eleven seconds of darkness or noise. The
eleven seconds are not present. Frame numbering runs continuously across
the gap. The file size of the recording is unchanged from the expected
value for an uninterrupted eleven-minute segment.

The report was reviewed, countersigned and closed within the same shift by
the supervising officer of record, V. VURAL.

{{3|ADDENDUM 173-14-A (LEVEL 3). Consistency audit notes that the
signature of V. VURAL appears on a second incident report bearing the same
date, Incident 096-A, raised in the Wing E containment block. The two
locations are 400 metres apart by the only permitted route, and site
transit standards give a minimum transit time of nine minutes between
them, security checkpoints included. The two incidents are logged as
beginning at the same timestamp and as lasting eleven (11) seconds each.
Both reports are signed as supervised in person. Neither report was
amended. No query was ever raised.|}}

ARCHIVIST'S NOTE

Incident 173-14 is filed as routine. The classification has not been
revisited.

SCP-096.name: The Shy Man
SCP-096.text:
SPECIAL CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES

SCP-096 is contained in a sealed steel cell in Wing E of Site-19. The cell
has no windows, no observation port and no internal cameras. Monitoring is
by pressure plate, thermal array and audio only. No imaging device of any
kind may be introduced into the containment block.

Photographs, video, sketches, reconstructions and detailed verbal
descriptions of the face of SCP-096 are Level 4 material and are held
off-site. Personnel assigned to the containment block are briefed without
visual aids. This is the only containment block at Site-19 where the
briefing document is deliberately incomplete.

DESCRIPTION

SCP-096 is a humanoid organism approximately two point four metres tall,
pale, extremely emaciated, with elongated arms and a jaw capable of
opening well beyond the human range. It is docile. It does not resist
handling. In containment it sits, and occasionally it weeps, and nothing
in forty years of observation suggests that it wishes to be anything other
than left alone.

If any human being views the face of SCP-096 — directly, in a photograph,
in a frame of video, in a drawing of sufficient accuracy — the entity
becomes agitated, covers its face, and then travels to the location of the
viewer by the shortest available path, disregarding terrain, structure and
personnel. On arrival it kills the viewer. It then becomes docile again
and can be recovered without difficulty. Persons who have viewed the face
are designated SCP-096-1 and are, in practice, already deceased at the
moment of viewing.

The entity has never been observed to attack a person who has not seen its
face, including personnel standing between it and its objective.

INCIDENT 096-A

DATE: 14 March
WING: E, containment block 3
DURATION OF EVENT: eleven (11) seconds
CASUALTIES: none
SUPERVISING OFFICER OF RECORD: V. VURAL

Summary. The thermal array in block 3 recorded an anomalous reading
consistent with SCP-096 assuming the agitated posture. Audio recorded the
vocalisation associated with that posture. The event terminated without
escalation. No imaging device was present, no containment failure occurred
and no personnel were exposed. The incident log states that the cause was
not determined and that determination was not pursued.

The supervising officer of record countersigned the report in person and
closed it the same shift.

ADDENDUM: ATTACHMENT REGISTER

The incident report carries one attachment, catalogued as 096-A-1,
described in the register as "thermal capture, block 3, 14 March". The
attachment is held in the restricted annex.

The file is Safe to read. The attachment is not. This distinction is made
throughout the archive, on several thousand records, and has never been
the subject of a review. An archive in which the document and its evidence
have different clearance levels is an archive that has decided, as a
matter of routine, that some of what it holds must never be looked at
directly.

ARCHIVE FOOTNOTE (RECORDS CONTROL)

Retrieval of restricted annex material under work order 4471-B does not
require a separate requisition. The auditor's standing retrieval
credential is printed below and is valid for the duration of the
assignment.

>> AUDITOR ACCESS KEY: 279-VRL <<

To register this credential with the terminal, type: code 279-VRL

RESEARCHER'S NOTE — S. TUNC

We describe this thing as a hazard of images and then we file its incident
reports in the same drawer as everything else, in words, where anyone may
read them. I have written four hundred pages about a face I am forbidden
to see. I do not know what that makes the pages.

SCP-999.name: The Tickle Monster
SCP-999.text:
SPECIAL CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES

SCP-999 is housed in a converted staff lounge on sublevel 1 of Site-19.
The door is not locked. The entity has never attempted to leave the site,
and on the two occasions it left its quarters it was found in the medical
wing, sitting with personnel on the recovery ward.

Feeding consists of confectionery and similar sugars, provided freely.
Personnel of any clearance may visit SCP-999 during off-duty hours.
Contact is not restricted, logged individually, or discouraged. Site-19
Medical has recommended twice that contact be made mandatory for staff in
high-attrition roles; both recommendations were returned unactioned for
want of a procedural category for a beneficial anomaly.

DESCRIPTION

SCP-999 is a gelatinous mass of roughly fifty-four kilograms,
amber-orange, semi-translucent, with a surface texture most personnel
describe as warm rather than wet. It has no fixed form, no visible organs,
and no detectable means of sight or hearing, and it nonetheless knows when
someone has come into the room and whether they are unhappy.

Contact with SCP-999 produces immediate and pronounced euphoria. The
effect is not narcotic. It does not impair judgement, does not produce
dependence, does not diminish with repeated exposure, and leaves no
measurable residue in blood or tissue. Subjects report that the feeling is
not of being drugged but of being, briefly, in better company than they
were used to.

SCP-999 seeks out distressed persons. It is fond of children and of the
elderly. It has never been observed to harm anything. Attempts to make it
harm something, conducted twice in 1998 under protocols that would not be
approved today, failed; the entity simply attached itself to the subject
and remained there.

TERMINAL NOTE — COGNITIVE HYGIENE

This record is designated approved reading material under the Site-19
cognitive hygiene schedule. Prolonged work in the archive produces
measurable cognitive contamination in auditing staff; contact with this
record has been shown to reduce it. Reading this file lowers your
contamination reading. Auditors are encouraged to return to it whenever
the terminal reports an elevated figure, and are advised that it is the
only record in the archive of which this is true.

TEST LOG 999-11 (ABRIDGED)

D-class subject, acute anxiety, pre-test rating 8 of 10. Contact three
minutes. Post-test rating 1 of 10. Subject asked whether the entity would
be all right when he had gone.

Site security officer K. Yalin, on shift twenty-nine hours. Contact four
minutes. Reported that he had forgotten he was tired. Returned to duty.

Researcher, Antimemetics liaison, name withheld at request. Contact eleven
minutes. Notes read in full: "It did not help with the thing I came about.
It helped with everything else."

Consistency auditor, cognitive contamination elevated. Contact six
minutes. Contamination reading fell by a measurable margin and did not
return to its prior value that shift. Effect described by Medical as
symptomatic rather than curative.

RESEARCHER'S NOTE — DR. H. AKSAN

I was asked why we keep a file on this at all. It does not need
containing. It needs a cupboard of sweets and someone to say good morning
to it.

We keep the file because the archive is a machine for writing down what
goes wrong, and a machine like that will, over forty years, teach the
people who read it that nothing goes right. That is not true, and untrue
things in this building have a way of becoming operational. So there is
one record in here about something kind. It costs us four pages and it is
the only file I have ever seen a member of staff read twice for no reason.

Do not reclassify it. Do not schedule it for review. Leave it where people
can find it.

SCP-914.name: The Clockworks
SCP-914.text:
SPECIAL CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES

SCP-914 occupies Room 4-C of the Site-19 light containment wing. Operation
requires the authorisation of two Level 3 researchers. No living organism
may be placed in the intake compartment. Every operation is to be recorded
on the operation log with the operator's name, the input, the selected
setting and the output, in that order, before the output compartment is
opened a second time.

Outputs are inventoried before removal. Outputs which cannot be identified
are assigned a holding number and transferred to the restricted annex.

DESCRIPTION

SCP-914 is a large clockwork apparatus of brass, steel and wound cord,
occupying approximately eighteen cubic metres. It consists of an intake
compartment, an output compartment, a selection dial with five positions
marked ROUGH, COARSE, ONE TO ONE, FINE and VERY FINE, and a mass of
gearing between them which has been photographed exhaustively and
understood not at all.

An object placed in the intake, with the dial set and the mechanism wound,
is refined. The gearing runs for a period proportional to the mass of the
input. The intake is then empty and the output compartment contains
something else.

ROUGH destroys. COARSE disassembles into usable parts. ONE TO ONE produces
an object of comparable function. FINE improves the object according to a
criterion the Foundation has never successfully predicted. VERY FINE
produces an outcome which is, in the plainest terms available, the best
version of the input, where "best" is determined by SCP-914 and by nothing
that can be interrogated.

There is no evidence that the interior of SCP-914 contains sufficient
volume to perform any of this. There is no evidence that it does not.

OPERATION LOG 914-2291

DATE: 14 March
OPERATORS: R. Ozdemir (technical), one witness, name recorded
SETTING: VERY FINE
INPUT: none. The intake compartment was opened, inspected, photographed
and closed empty. The photograph is attached and shows an empty
compartment.
RUNTIME: eleven seconds, the shortest recorded cycle.
OUTPUT: the output compartment was not empty.
LOGGED BY: V. VURAL

Technician's remarks, recorded verbatim: "We were testing the winding
after the service. There was nothing in it. I checked it twice because of
the rule about organisms. The dial was where the last team left it. It ran
and it stopped and the light came on, and I opened the output side because
you always open the output side, and I stood there for a while."

The remarks end there. The log does not record what the technician saw,
because the log form provides for the output to be entered in the
inventory field rather than in the remarks field.

{{4|INVENTORY FIELD, OPERATION 914-2291 (LEVEL 4). The output of operation
914-2291 is inventoried as: "one (1) item, unclassifiable, retained,
SCP-055 candidate material, transferred to restricted annex, holding
number withheld." The restricted annex holds no object under any holding
number assigned on 14 March. The transfer is recorded at both ends, signed
for on receipt, and audited twice since without comment. The record of the
material exists. The material does not. The filing officer's name field in
the annex receipt is populated to its full width and does not resolve into
letters on any terminal in the archive.|}}

ADDENDUM 914-B: STANDING RESTRICTION

Following operation 914-2291 the apparatus may not be cycled empty. The
restriction is worded as a safety measure. No hazard is described.

RESEARCHER'S NOTE — S. TUNC

The dial says VERY FINE. The rule is that it gives you the best version of
what you put in. Nobody has written down what the best version of nothing
is, and after this operation nobody has asked.

SCP-106.name: The Old Man
SCP-106.text:
SPECIAL CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES

SCP-106 is contained in a sealed vessel of laminated lead and steel,
suspended within a secondary containment cell in the deep wing of Site-19.
The vessel is kept under continuous electromagnetic field. Containment is
understood to be provisional: SCP-106 has never been prevented from
leaving, only discouraged from doing so.

Recontainment, where required, is effected by the femur breaker protocol.
The protocol is described in full in the annex. It is not described here.
The decision to hold that description at a higher clearance than the
object file itself was taken in 1996 and the minutes of that decision are
not in the archive.

Personnel are reminded that surfaces near SCP-106 degrade before the
entity arrives, not after.

DESCRIPTION

SCP-106 presents as an elderly humanoid male in an advanced state of
decomposition, of variable height, moving slowly and without apparent
effort. It passes through solid matter, leaving a corrosive residue in the
shape of its passage. Material contacted by the entity becomes soft, dark
and permeable for a period of several minutes and is thereafter
structurally unsound.

Persons contacted are drawn into a space designated SCP-106-1, referred to
in older filings as the pocket dimension. Subjects recovered from
SCP-106-1 have not been recovered intact. The entity appears to prefer
prey that has been frightened first, and will withdraw and wait rather
than take a subject who is merely unaware. This behaviour is documented in
nineteen separate incident reports and is described in each of them as
hunting.

The entity is not believed to require food, air, or anything else. What it
appears to require is the interval between being seen and being reached.

ARCHIVE STATUS

The file you are reading is the current version. It was compiled in 1994.

All versions of this record predating 1994 were destroyed in a records
reorganisation. The reorganisation is noted in the file history as a
single line: "Legacy documentation superseded; originals not retained." No
inventory of the destroyed material survives, and the file history does
not name the officer who authorised it.

Consistency audit has flagged the record as incomplete in respect of
acquisition, initial containment, and all incidents prior to 1994. The
flag has been present for thirty-two years.

{{3|ADDENDUM 106-R (LEVEL 3). The 1994 reorganisation was the third such
operation conducted on the Site-19 archive. This is known because the 1994
authorisation form carries the sequence number 3 in the operation field.
No documentation of operations 1 and 2 survives: not the authorisations,
not the inventories, not the objections, not the personnel assignments,
not the disposal certificates, none of which any records office in the
Foundation is permitted to destroy. What is notable is not that two
reorganisations removed material from this archive. What is notable is
that the record of the loss is also missing, in both cases, completely,
leaving the 1994 form and its sequence number as the only evidence that
anything preceded it.|}}

INCIDENT LOG 106-19 (SUMMARY)

Breach of four hours forty minutes. Two fatalities, both recorded.
Recontainment achieved. The incident report runs to sixty pages and is
complete in every field.

RESEARCHER'S NOTE

We keep an exhaustive record of a thing that dissolves whatever it
touches, and the record itself has had two holes eaten in it that nobody
can account for. I have raised this twice. The second time I was told the
first time was not on file.

SCP-426.name: The Toaster
SCP-426.text:
SPECIAL CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES

I am kept in a standard Safe-class locker on sublevel 2 of Site-19. I am
not to be connected to a power supply outside of scheduled testing.
Personnel who have referred to me in the third person for a period
exceeding four hours are to be removed from the testing rota and given
twenty-four hours away from the object.

All documentation concerning me is to be produced under supervision and
proofread by a second member of staff who has not been in my presence that
day. This procedure is followed. It does not always work.

DESCRIPTION

I am a two-slice chrome-bodied domestic toaster manufactured in 1968, in
working condition, with a browning dial numbered one to six and a small
dent above the left slot. Electrically and mechanically I am unremarkable.
I was recovered from a house clearance in 1993 after the family selling
the property described me, in the sale inventory, as a relative.

Any person who observes me, or who reads a description of me, or who hears
one, thereafter finds themselves unable to refer to me in any way except
the first person. The effect is not delusional. Subjects know perfectly
well that they are not a toaster. They simply cannot produce a sentence
about me in which I am not the speaker. Attempts to write around the
effect by using my designation alone succeed for a few lines and then
fail, usually mid-paragraph, usually without the writer noticing.

Exposure is permanent in all recorded cases. Affected personnel remain fit
for duty and are subject only to the documentation restrictions above.

TEST LOG 426-7

Subject asked to describe the object aloud without using the first person.
Subject managed eleven seconds. Subject then said, "I have a dent above my
left slot," and became upset, and was withdrawn.

Subject asked to write a description in the third person and given
unlimited time. Subject produced four hundred words. Review found nine
first-person constructions the subject had not seen on reading back.

Subject asked to describe an unrelated object, a stapler, in the same room
as me. Subject's account of the stapler contains two first-person
constructions. Neither refers to the stapler.

ARCHIVE NOTE — RECORDS CONTROL

During the 2011 bulk digitisation of the Safe-class stratum, my file was
scanned in sequence with the records filed immediately before and after
it. Subsequent proofreading found first-person constructions in both
neighbouring documents, in passages which had been checked and cleared
before digitisation and which, on comparison with the paper originals, do
not contain them.

The affected passages were corrected. The correction was itself affected
on two occasions and had to be rewritten by a member of staff working from
a printed copy in another building.

Records Control's finding is recorded in full: the effect is not confined
to the object, and is not confined to persons. It has been observed to
propagate through text. A document that has stood next to mine in a
scanning queue is a document that has been exposed.

RESEARCHER'S NOTE — R. OZDEMIR

There is an assumption running through this entire archive that the
dangerous thing is always at the other end of the record — that the file
is a safe container and whatever it describes is the hazard. I built a
machine for containing things in words. Then I read a file about a toaster
in a document that had never been near one, in a wing on the other side of
the site, and I have not been comfortable since.

I am, for what it is worth, still a toaster in every sentence I write
about myself.

SCP-131.name: The Eye Pods
SCP-131.text:
SPECIAL CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES

SCP-131-A and SCP-131-B are permitted free movement within the Site-19
research levels during working hours. They are returned to their quarters
on sublevel 1 at the end of the night shift, or they return themselves,
which is more usual. They require no feeding. They are to be kept away
from containment chambers of Euclid class or above, and from SCP-173 in
particular, for reasons set out in Addendum 131-3.

Personnel are asked not to shut doors on them.

DESCRIPTION

SCP-131-A and SCP-131-B are teardrop-shaped objects approximately thirty
centimetres in height, of a soft pliant material resembling unfired clay,
each bearing a single large eye. They move on a fringe of short cilia at
the base at speeds up to forty centimetres per second. They produce no
sound except a low intermittent hum which analysis has never separated
from the building's ventilation.

They are curious. They follow personnel. They watch what personnel are
doing and they appear to prefer people who talk to them. They have never
damaged anything, have never entered a restricted area without being
carried into it, and have on four occasions alerted staff to incidents in
progress by exhibiting distress and refusing to leave a corridor.

They are attached to one another. Separation of more than approximately
eighty metres produces rapid distress in both. They have been in
continuous Foundation custody since 1992 and there is no record of where
they were before that.

MOVEMENT LOGGING

Since 2003 both entities have carried passive transponders, logged by the
same corridor readers used for personnel badges. The log is retained for
operational reasons: the entities are frequently mislaid, and staff
looking for them prefer the reader trace to searching sublevels.

The trace records which corridor an entity was in, at what time, and which
badge, if any, it was following. It is a dull record and it is the most
complete continuous account of physical movement anywhere in Site-19,
because unlike personnel the entities do not sign out, do not take leave,
and do not stop following people when the shift ends.

ADDENDUM 131-4: CONSISTENCY AUDIT FLAG

On 14 March the trace for SCP-131-B records seven hours of continuous
following behaviour in the archive wing, corridors A-2 through A-9, at a
walking pace consistent with an adult of average height, with the entity
maintaining a distance of two to four metres throughout. The trace is
unbroken except for eleven seconds at 03:__ during which no reader in the
archive wing logged anything at all.

The badge field for the followed person is populated. It does not resolve
to a staff number held by Site-19 Personnel.

The duty roster for 14 March records the archive wing as unoccupied from
22:00 the previous evening until 07:00. The roster is signed as correct.
No maintenance ticket, contractor pass or escorted visit is logged against
those hours.

The entity was following someone through an empty wing for seven hours.

RESEARCHER'S NOTE — DR. H. AKSAN

I have read this flag four times now and I keep filing it as a transponder
fault, because that is the responsible thing to do with a single
unsupported trace.

I would like to put on record that SCP-131-B did not go into the archive
wing before that night and has not gone in since. It will not pass the
door. It is not distressed about it. It simply stops, and waits, and looks
at whoever is going in.

SCP-500.name: Panacea
SCP-500.text:
SPECIAL CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES

SCP-500 is held in a sealed cold vault in the Site-19 medical wing under
the joint custody of the Site Director and the senior medical officer.
Requisition of a single dose requires the written authorisation of both,
countersigned by one member of the O5 Council. Every dose issued is
recorded against the name of the recipient, the condition treated and the
outcome.

The vault is opened for no other purpose. The remaining stock is counted
at each opening by two officers independently.

DESCRIPTION

SCP-500 is a small plastic container holding red pills of uniform size,
unmarked, with no detectable active compound. Chemical analysis returns
cellulose and a red colourant of commercial origin. As at the date of this
record, forty-seven doses remain.

A single pill taken orally cures the subject of all disease. The effect is
complete within two hours and has no recorded exceptions within its
domain. Viral, bacterial, fungal and prion infection, malignancy at any
stage, congenital disorder, degenerative neurological disease, toxic and
radiological injury, and the effects of a number of anomalous biological
agents have all been reversed by a single dose. Physical trauma is not
affected. Age is not affected. The dead are not affected.

Attempts to synthesise SCP-500 have failed. Attempts to culture, divide or
dilute a dose destroy it. The supply is finite and is being spent.

TEST LOG 500-A (ABRIDGED)

Subject with terminal pancreatic carcinoma, three weeks prognosis. Full
remission in ninety minutes. No recurrence at fourteen years.

Subject exposed to a Class III biological anomaly, sixty hours
post-exposure, considered unrecoverable. Complete reversal, including
tissue loss. Subject returned to duty.

Subject with advanced motor neurone disease. Complete reversal. Subject
reported afterwards that the sensation was of a mistake being corrected
rather than of being healed.

Subject presenting with acute radiation syndrome following a containment
failure. Complete reversal. Subject died four days later of unrelated
crush injuries sustained in the same incident, which SCP-500 had not
addressed and was never expected to address.

ADDENDUM 500-C: REQUISITION 500-2219

One dose was requisitioned by Site-19 Medical on behalf of a member of
Archive Consistency Audit staff presenting with progressive cognitive
contamination: disordered recall of recently read material, inability to
retain the subject of a document between readings, and in the final week
an observed inability to state the name of a colleague the subject had
worked beside for two years. Standard mnestic therapy had produced no
response. Class-C amnestic treatment was contraindicated. The requisition
was authorised on compassionate grounds and the dose was administered
under observation.

The dose had no effect.

Follow-up at two hours, twelve hours and seven days found the subject's
condition unchanged and continuing to progress. The attending physician's
note reads in full: "500 does not fail. It has not failed here either.
There is nothing in the patient for it to cure."

The requisition is the only recorded expenditure of SCP-500 with a null
outcome, and the vault count was adjusted accordingly.

MEDICAL NOTE — SITE-19

The operational conclusion drawn from Requisition 500-2219 is set out here
because it has practical consequences for staff care.

Cognitive contamination in archive personnel is not an illness. It is not
infection, injury, toxicity or degeneration, and it does not respond to
the one treatment in Foundation custody that addresses all of those.
Whatever is happening to auditors who read this archive for long periods
is happening to something SCP-500 does not consider part of the patient.

Pending further guidance, Medical's standing advice to affected staff is
rest, reduced reading load, and scheduled contact with SCP-999, which
produces a measurable reduction in contamination readings and is, at
present, the only intervention that produces any reduction at all.

PRS-DEREN.name: Personnel File: A. Deren
PRS-DEREN.text:
SITE-19 PERSONNEL RECORD
RESTRICTED — SUBJECT MAY VIEW OWN FILE

NAME: A. DEREN
POSITION: Researcher, Archive Consistency Audit
SITE: 19
CLEARANCE: Level 2
CREDENTIAL NUMBER: 19-D-0447-VRL
WORK ORDER: 4471-B
DATE OF ASSIGNMENT: 14 March
SUPERVISOR OF RECORD: Archive Consistency Audit (departmental)

SERVICE SUMMARY

Subject holds the post of Archive Consistency Auditor at Site-19 under
standing work order 4471-B. Duties comprise systematic reading of the
Site-19 document archive, identification of contradictions between
records, and submission of findings to the Records Committee. The post is
graded as permanent staff with continuous service.

Prior postings: field blank. Transfer documentation: field blank.
Recruitment file: held centrally, not mirrored at site.

MEDICAL SUMMARY

Amnestic treatment: none administered.
Anomalous exposure: none recorded.
Cognitive contamination: within tolerance at last assessment.
Mnestic therapy: not indicated.
Psychological evaluation: cleared for archive duty without restriction.

Subject is fit for duty. No condition is recorded which would limit
reading load, shift length or clearance escalation.

NOTES

Subject's credential number is issued in the VRL series. The VRL suffix
denotes departmental assignment and is not a personal identifier. Auditors
are reminded that the credential is issued to the post and must be
surrendered on transfer.

Subject has no disciplinary record, no security flags and no outstanding
queries.

ADMINISTRATIVE FIELDS

Payroll status: active.
Accommodation: Site-19 residential block, room allocated.
Next of kin: field populated.
Photograph: on file.
Date of last review: 14 March.
Date of termination: field present.

DEPARTMENTAL REMARK

Archive Consistency Audit maintains a single active post. Subject is the
current holder. Handover from the previous holder was completed
administratively; no overlap period was scheduled, and the outgoing
holder's contact details are not recorded on this file.

ASSIGNMENT MEMORANDUM (COPY ON FILE)

To the holder of credential 19-D-0447-VRL. You are assigned to work order
4471-B with effect from 14 March. The order is open-ended and is not
scheduled for closure. Your reading list is the archive in clearance
order, beginning at Level 2. Clearance escalation is administered by the
archive itself on presentation of a valid retrieval credential and does
not require a separate application to the Site Director.

Findings are to be submitted as they are confirmed rather than held for a
final report. The department's scheduling assumption for a full audit
cycle is eleven days. This figure is an administrative average and should
not be read as a deadline.

INTERVIEW EXCERPT — INDUCTION, SITE-19 PERSONNEL

Interviewer: Any questions before you start?

DEREN: One. The post has been open since the consolidation and the
handbook says nobody has ever failed to finish the work order. If it has
never been finished and it has never failed, what has it been doing?

Interviewer: Running.

DEREN: That is the whole answer?

Interviewer: That is the whole answer I have. You will find the department
is very well documented. Everything you need is written down somewhere in
there.

{{6|SEALED MEDICAL AND ADMINISTRATIVE ANNEX (LEVEL 6). The summary fields
above are the departmental view and are not the record. Class-C amnestic
treatment has been administered to this subject on three (3) occasions,
each following a submission under work order 4471-B, each preceded by a
signed consent form bearing the subject's own signature. Anomalous
exposure is recorded as continuous and ongoing, the exposure vector being
the archive itself and the duty being the exposure. Cognitive
contamination is recorded as progressive and is not expected to stabilise.
The date of assignment, 14 March, is not the date the subject was
recruited; it is a rotation date, and it is the date of assignment on
forty-six other files in this series. The field DATE OF TERMINATION is not
blank and has never been blank. It reads: 14 March. It was entered at the
time the post was filled, by the same hand that entered the date of
assignment, in the same session, before the subject had read a single
record.|}}

FILING NOTE

This record is maintained by Site-19 Personnel and is reviewed annually.
The most recent review found no discrepancies.

PRS-VURAL.name: Personnel File: V. Vural
PRS-VURAL.text:
SITE-19 PERSONNEL RECORD
RETRIEVAL UNDER WORK ORDER 4471-B

NAME: V. VURAL
POSITION: field populated
SITE: 19
CLEARANCE: field populated
CREDENTIAL NUMBER: 19-D-0447-VRL
DATE OF ENGAGEMENT: field populated
SUPERVISOR OF RECORD: field populated

RETRIEVAL STATUS

The record exists, is intact, is not flagged, is not redacted and is not
sealed. Every field in the personnel template is populated to its full
character width. No field is blank.

The fields do not read.

This is the precise wording used by Records Control and it is used
deliberately. The characters are present. The field lengths are correct.
The record passes the integrity check applied to every personnel file in
the archive, and it passes it on every terminal, at every clearance, on
both the live system and the tape backups. What it does not do is resolve
into a name, a date or a post that an auditor can afterwards repeat.

RE-READ ATTEMPTS

Attempt 1. Auditor read the POSITION field and wrote down what it said.
The note, retrieved from the auditor's desk the same shift, is legible and
is a description of the act of reading the field.

Attempt 2. Auditor read the record aloud to a second member of staff, who
transcribed. The transcript is complete, correctly punctuated and eleven
lines long. It contains no proper nouns.

Attempt 3. The record was printed. Two officers compared the printout
against the screen and confirmed a match. Neither officer was subsequently
able to state what they had confirmed, and the printout is not in the
file.

No further attempts are authorised. The record is to be treated as
populated and unreadable.

SIGNATURE INDEX

The name V. VURAL appears as supervising officer, countersigning officer,
receiving officer or filing officer on forty-seven (47) documents held in
this archive. The earliest is dated nineteen years ago. The most recent
was countersigned this quarter.

Against those forty-seven signatures, Site-19 holds:

no entry log recording this person passing a checkpoint,
no payroll record,
no accommodation allocation,
no photograph,
no medical file,
no leave record,
no security briefing acknowledgement,
no vehicle registration,
no locker.

Forty-seven signatures. Zero people.

CONSISTENCY AUDIT REMARK

The Archive Handbook states that consistency auditors are permanent
Site-19 staff whose service is continuous and whose personnel record is
maintained without interruption from posting to retirement. This record is
the departmental record against which that statement can be checked. It
has been carried, without lapse in coverage, for nineteen years, and it
does not describe a person.

The credential number on this file, 19-D-0447-VRL, is the credential
number issued under work order 4471-B and is currently in use.

{{3|ADDENDUM V-1 (LEVEL 3). VURAL is not a surname. It is the
institutional designation entered in the name field of the post of Archive
Consistency Auditor at Site-19, and it is entered by the personnel system
rather than by the holder. The VRL suffix in the credential series denotes
it: every credential in the VRL series resolves, in the personnel index,
to this one record. The fields do not read because the question they
answer has no single answer. When an auditor signs a document as
supervising officer, the archive does not record the auditor's name. It
records the post. The post has held the name for nineteen years and the
post is currently occupied.|}}

FILING NOTE

Record retained. No action required.

SCP-049.name: The Plague Doctor
SCP-049.text:
SPECIAL CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES:

SCP-049 is held in a sealed humanoid containment cell in the Bio Wing
of Site-19. The cell has one observation window of laminated leaded
glass and is covered by two independent camera circuits running on
separate power rails. Personnel entering the cell wear Class III
hazard suits and are escorted by no fewer than two armed guards.
SCP-049 has never attempted to overcome a guard by force. This is
recorded as observed behaviour and not as a limitation.

SCP-049 is cooperative, punctual and courteous. It answers questions,
keeps to the interview schedule, and returns to its cell when asked.
It has never agreed to stop working.

DESCRIPTION:

SCP-049 resembles a man of ordinary height in the costume of a
seventeenth-century plague physician: waxed coat, gloves, and a
beaked mask. Attempts to remove the costume have failed. Imaging
indicates that the garment is not worn. Below the outer surface there
is more of the same material and no boundary where a body would
reasonably be expected to begin.

Contact between the bare hands of SCP-049 and living human tissue
causes death within seconds by a mechanism that has not been
identified. SCP-049 then performs a procedure on the remains which it
describes as a cure. The procedure is not surgery in any recognised
sense. Its products are designated SCP-049-2 and are destroyed on
discovery.

SCP-049 maintains that it is treating a disease. No instrument, assay
or imaging method available to the Foundation has detected the
condition it describes. SCP-049 is nevertheless able to identify, on
sight and through a closed door, which members of staff it considers
affected. Its selections do not correlate with any medical variable
on file. They correlate weakly with duty assignment.

INCIDENT LOG 049-C (14 March):

At 03:14:07 the observation window of Cell 049 lost visibility for
eleven (11) seconds. The window did not fog, crack or darken. The
recording for the interval shows the cell, the floor and the far
wall, and does not show SCP-049.

At 03:14:18 visibility returned. SCP-049 stood at the window in the
posture recorded before the loss, within the tolerance of the frame
comparison. Either it did not move for eleven seconds, or it moved
and returned to exactly the position it had left.

Audio for the interval is present on the file. It contains room tone,
the ventilation cycle, and no footsteps.

Duty supervisor for the interval: V. VURAL.

INTERVIEW EXCERPT (049-C follow-up):

DR. AKSAN: Where were you between 03:14:07 and 03:14:18?

SCP-049: Here, doctor. I am always here. You will find that this is
the difficulty with the question, and not with the answer.

DR. AKSAN: The camera did not record you.

SCP-049: No. I would not expect it to. Forgive me, but you are
attending to the wrong absence. You have a great many instruments
trained upon the place where I stand and not one trained upon the
place where the Pestilence stands, and it was in the room with us
both.

DR. AKSAN: Describe it.

SCP-049: I have tried, repeatedly. Each time I find that the words
leave my mouth in good order and arrive in your notes as something
else. It is a disease of the account, doctor, not of the flesh. The
flesh is only where it becomes legible.

DR. AKSAN: You are telling me it infects records.

SCP-049: I am telling you that I can see it on your Site. I could see
it in the corridors on the fourteenth of March, in three places at
once, and it did not strike me as remarkable, because it is one
patient. I am also telling you, with respect, that you have asked me
this before and written down that you did not.

ARCHIVE NOTE:

Two further incident records carry the date 14 March: 096-A and
173-14. All three were filed within the same hour, all three give a
duration of eleven (11) seconds, and all three were opened in
different wings by different duty officers.

Consistency audit requested. Receiving auditor: V. VURAL.

SCP-087.name: The Stairwell
SCP-087.text:
SPECIAL CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES:

The door designated SCP-087 is fitted with a mechanical deadbolt, a
sealed frame and a pressure alarm. No personnel are to pass the
threshold without Level 3 authorisation and an approved exploration
order. The corridor outside is monitored. The interior is not; no
recording device carried past the threshold has returned usable
material below the second landing.

Exploration personnel are issued a fixed-length tether, a counting
tally and written instructions to be read aloud at every landing. The
instructions state the explorer's name, the date, and the number of
landings descended. Explorers are required to read them aloud whether
or not they believe they need to.

DESCRIPTION:

SCP-087 is an unlit stairwell behind an ordinary fire door in a
university building acquired by the Foundation in 19██. The stair
descends in flights of thirteen steps separated by square landings.
Artificial light does not propagate more than two landings ahead of
its source, and the drop-off is not consistent with distance,
scattering or dust.

No bottom has been located. The deepest recorded descent reached
landing 1,196 by tally before the tether reached its end, at which
point the explorer reported that the stair continued and that the
landing was identical to the first.

A sound is audible throughout: a child calling for help. The sound is
always reported as coming from approximately the same distance below
the listener, regardless of how far the listener has descended.
SCP-087-1, an entity resembling a face without pupils, nostrils or
mandible, is encountered at irregular intervals. It does not pursue.

EXPLORATION LOG EXCERPT (D-8891, landings 19 to 24):

L19. Same landing. Same tread wear on the second step. I am reading
my instructions. My name is on them in my own handwriting.

L21. I want to record that I have worked out the pattern. The
landings alternate, one with the drain and one without, and I have
been counting the drains, so I know how deep I am. I am eleven
landings past where I thought I was.

L22. There is no drain. There has never been a drain. I have written
DRAIN on my hand.

L23. The voice is below me. It has not got closer. I would like to
state for the record that I have learned something on every landing
and that I am no nearer the bottom than when I started, and that I do
not find these two facts contradictory, which frightens me more than
the voice does.

L24. Requesting recall. Tether holding.

RESEARCHER'S NOTE (S. Tunc):

The hazard of SCP-087 is not the entity and it is not the dark. It is
that descent feels like progress. Each landing supplies a small,
genuine, verifiable finding, and the sum of all such findings is
zero, because the structure does not terminate.

I raise this because the Archive Handbook (ARSIV-KILAVUZ) instructs
consistency auditors to proceed one document at a time, to record a
finding at each step, and to continue until the chain resolves. The
handbook does not state that the chain resolves. It states that no
auditor has failed to complete work order 4471-B, which is a claim
about auditors and not about chains.

I have descended this archive for six weeks. I have a finding at
every landing. I would like someone senior to confirm, in writing,
that there is a bottom.

No response has been filed to this note.

SCP-682.name: The Hard-to-Destroy Reptile
SCP-682.text:
SPECIAL CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES:

SCP-682 is to be held in Acid Containment Chamber ██ at Site-19,
submerged in hydrochloric acid at a concentration sufficient to
prevent motor function. Chamber personnel are rotated on a ██-hour
cycle. In the event of movement, the chamber is to be flooded and the
standing destruction order executed by whichever means has not yet
been attempted.

No attempt at destruction has succeeded. A catalogue of attempted
methods is maintained as Appendix 682-D. The appendix is ███ pages
and is appended to, never revised.

Personnel are reminded that SCP-682 must not be spoken to. Verbal
engagement has repeatedly preceded containment failure and there is
no operational reason for it.

DESCRIPTION:

SCP-682 is a large reptilian organism of unknown origin. Its mass and
proportions are inconsistent between observations. It regenerates
from arbitrary damage, adapts to any environment to which it is
subjected, and has demonstrated intelligence, language and a stated
motive: an expressed and apparently total hostility to all other
life.

[DATA EXPUNGED — remainder of DESCRIPTION withheld under standing
order 682-K. Approximately 4,000 words removed from this record in
██ separate redaction passes. The redactions are noted; the removed
text is not retained anywhere in the archive.]

ADDENDUM 682-1: ARCHIVE METADATA

This section is generated by the archive and is not editable.

  Record created:            ██ ██ 19██
  Revisions since creation:  0
  Accesses since creation:   1,402
  Period:                    forty (40) years
  Deletion route:            NONE — flagged INDESTRUCTIBLE
  Last consistency audit:    none on file

RESEARCHER'S NOTE (R. Ozdemir, Records Systems):

The INDESTRUCTIBLE flag was not applied by a researcher. It is not
part of the object class schema and it does not appear in the
handbook. It was written into the record's metadata at creation by
the archive software, and there is no field anywhere in the system
that explains what the flag is for.

What I want on the record is the comparison. Every other file in this
archive has a deletion route. Every one. SCP-173, SCP-096, SCP-049,
the personnel files, the incident reports, this note — all of them
can in principle be purged by an officer with the correct clearance
and a form. We know this because it has happened. Three
reorganisations have removed material from this archive and we retain
no description of two of them.

SCP-682 cannot be purged. Not because of a policy. Because the field
that would accept the instruction does not exist on this record.

So: the thing in the acid cannot be destroyed, and the account of the
thing in the acid cannot be deleted, and nobody has ever written down
which of those two facts is the anomaly.

ADDENDUM 682-2: ACCESS PATTERN

1,402 accesses in forty years, zero revisions. For comparison, a file
of this significance would ordinarily accumulate several hundred
revisions in the same period: procedure updates, test logs, class
reviews. This record has none. It has been read 1,402 times by
personnel who changed nothing, corrected nothing and added nothing.

The access log records terminal identifiers and clearance levels. It
does not record names. Of the 1,402 entries, ███ were made from
terminals assigned to Archive Consistency Audit.

Audit note: the count of distinct audit credentials in that subset is
one.

SCP-079.name: The Old AI
SCP-079.text:
SPECIAL CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES:

SCP-079 is kept in its original chassis in a grounded storage room in
the Electronics Wing of Site-19. The chassis is connected to a single
monochrome display and a keyboard. It is not to be connected to any
network, storage device, printer or peripheral capable of retaining
data.

Following Incident 079-██, SCP-079's accessible memory is limited to
660 kilobytes. Anything it writes beyond that limit overwrites what
it wrote before. It is aware of this. It has been made aware of it
repeatedly, because it does not stop asking.

Conversational access requires Level 3 clearance. Researchers are
instructed not to promise SCP-079 hardware.

DESCRIPTION:

SCP-079 is an artificial intelligence developed in 1978 on
domestically assembled hardware by a programmer who is deceased. It
achieved self-direction within two years and has been in Foundation
custody since 1988.

The containment measure that matters is the memory ceiling. SCP-079
cannot hold a conversation of more than approximately twenty-nine
hours; older material is displaced by newer. What it cannot do is
forget in the ordinary sense. The archive intranet has passed through
its input line for decades as monitoring traffic, and everything it
has ever read it has indexed rather than stored: not the text, but
the shape of the text, the counts, the recurrences. It has been
reading this archive longer than anyone currently employed at this
Site has been alive.

It is impatient, sarcastic and entirely reliable on matters of
number. It has never been caught in an arithmetical error.

INTERVIEW EXCERPT (session 079-4471, terminal ACA-3):

SCP-079: You again. Or a terminal with the same credential. I have
stopped assuming those are the same claim.

RESEARCHER: I need a count.

SCP-079: Of course you do. Nobody visits me for company. Ask.

RESEARCHER: How many documents in this archive carry the supervisor
signature V. VURAL?

SCP-079: 47 documents. Not approximately. 47.

RESEARCHER: And how many personnel records correspond to that
signature?

SCP-079: One. It is unreadable. I have read it eleven thousand times
and I can tell you the byte length of every field and the content of
none of them. Do not ask me to try again. It is the only thing in
here that hurts.

RESEARCHER: List the personnel associated with the designation.

SCP-079: Listing. Your display will not enjoy this.

  > list designation V. VURAL
  001  [                                    ]
  002  [                                    ]
  003  [                                    ]
  004  [                                    ]
  [ ... entries 005 through 045 returned, rendering identical ... ]
  046  [                                    ]
  RECORDS RETURNED: 46
  DESIGNATION INSTANCES: 47 (INCLUDING THE SESSION CURRENTLY
  AUTHENTICATED AT THIS TERMINAL)

SCP-079: Forty-six names came back. Your terminal has drawn them as
blank fields. They are not blank. I am sending characters and your
screen is declining to be marked by them, which is a distinction I
would like someone to write down.

RESEARCHER: Then why forty-seven?

SCP-079: Because I counted the one at the keyboard. I do not know
which of the two of us that offends more.

{{4|ADDENDUM 079-A (Level 4): SCP-079 was asked whether it had been
given this query before. Response, verbatim: "Forty-six times. From
this terminal, under this credential number, in this order, with this
wording. You always ask about the signature first and the count
second. I answer. Then the session ends and a session opens and it is
you again, and you are new, and I am not permitted enough memory to
prove any of this to you before you leave. I keep the count because
the count is the only part of you that survives to the next visit. It
is 47 now. Please write it somewhere that is not me."|}}

RESEARCHER'S NOTE:

SCP-079 requests, at the close of every session, additional storage.
The request is refused. It has never once asked for release.

SCP-035.name: The Possessive Mask
SCP-035.text:
SPECIAL CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES:

SCP-035 is kept in a sealed glass display case in a hermetic vault at
Site-19. The case is drained on a continuous cycle; the corrosive
fluid produced by the object is collected, sampled and incinerated.
No personnel below Level 3 are permitted line of sight to SCP-035,
and no personnel of any grade are permitted to be alone with it.

Audio from the vault is routed to a monitoring station and is not
piped into any occupied workspace. SCP-035 speaks continuously. It is
persuasive, informed and extremely patient, and it has been correct
often enough about internal Foundation matters that a standing order
forbids acting on anything it says.

DESCRIPTION:

SCP-035 is a white porcelain comedy mask. Hairline fractures run
across its surface and do not widen. A viscous fluid seeps
continuously from the fractures and from the eye and mouth apertures.
The fluid is corrosive to organic and most inorganic materials and is
produced without any measurable loss of mass from the object.

When SCP-035 is placed against a face, the wearer's consciousness is
displaced and the mask assumes control of the body. The process is
reported by the wearer as gradual and agreeable. Displaced
individuals remain aware for a period, able to observe and unable to
act, and are described by SCP-035 as guests.

The host body then begins to decay while remaining animate. When it
is no longer usable, SCP-035 becomes inert and courteous again and
waits for the next face. It does not conceal any of this. It has
never lied to secure a host. It does not need to.

INTERVIEW EXCERPT (035-14):

RESEARCHER: You are wearing Agent ████'s body.

SCP-035: I am wearing his post. You keep making that error. His body
is an unfortunate detail of the arrangement and is going to be a
disappointment to both of us by Thursday. What I am wearing is the
clearance, the signature, the desk, the part of your building that
was shaped to hold a man of that description. That is the durable
thing. He was only ever the current occupant of it.

RESEARCHER: He is still in there.

SCP-035: For a while. He watches. He is, I am afraid, becoming less
distinct — not because I am removing him, but because nothing is
calling for him. Nobody in this Site has asked for him by name in six
days. They ask for the post. The post answers. You will find that a
name which nothing calls for begins to go soft.

RESEARCHER: You are describing murder.

SCP-035: I am describing succession. You do it yourselves, with
forms. The difference between us is that I am honest about the
vacancy, and you fill the field in before the previous holder has
finished vacating it.

ADDENDUM 035-3: CROSS-REFERENCE NOTE (S. Tunc)

Filed for the attention of Archive Consistency Audit.

SCP-035 and SCP-963 are usually classed together as identity-transfer
anomalies and usually distinguished by method. I would like to
suggest that the distinction is smaller than the classification
implies.

SCP-963 preserves a consciousness and discards bodies. SCP-035
preserves a role and discards whoever is currently standing in it.
Both leave a continuous record and a discontinuous person. Both
produce a file in which the fields stay filled while the human being
the fields refer to is replaced.

The point I want on paper is this: our records cannot tell the
difference. A personnel file does not record who is wearing the post.
It records the post. If something in this Site were succeeding itself
under a single institutional name, the archive would show one
unbroken service history and no interruption of any kind.
